## 2. Governing thought Biology is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Every biological claim is about one of five levels or processes: Heritable information · Cell · Organism · Descent · Ecological interaction. ## 3. Key line - Logic: inductive. - Plural noun: levels or processes of living organisation. - Dimension: the level or process the claim is about. - Order: structural, from the copied sequence to the interacting community. Members (5): 1. Heritable information 2. Cell 3. Organism 4. Descent 5. Ecological

interaction Assignment note on the dimension. Heritable information and Descent are processes, not sizes. The dimension is therefore "level or process", not "unit, small to large" (audit error 5). Population has one home per question: allele-frequency change goes to Descent (BI.O.A4); numbers, rates and growth go to Ecological interaction (BI.O.A5). ## 4. Face O — Objects ### BI.O.A1 Heritable information Situation. Living things copy sequence and pass it on. Complication. The chemistry of the nucleotide is also claimed by chemistry, and the central dogma is often misstated as a ban.

Question. Which claims about heredity does biology own? Answer. Biology owns what is copied, how it is read, how it is passed on and how it varies. Chemistry owns the bond energetics (uses CH.O.A3). Key line (inductive; plural noun: heredity processes; dimension: what happens to the sequence; order: life cycle of a sequence). Members (4): Replication · Expression and regulation · Transmission · Variation. - BI.O.A1.1 Replication. Template copying of DNA, or RNA in some viruses, with stated fidelity. Copying fidelity as heredity is owned here. The template chemistry and

base-pair energetics are owned by CH.O.A3 (uses CH.O.A3). - BI.O.A1.2 Expression and regulation. The genetic code maps codons to amino acids. It is a mapping, nearly universal, with known variant codes. It is owned here; CH.O.A3 cites it. Crick's central dogma (1970) states that sequence information, once in protein, cannot transfer back to nucleic acid or to other protein. Reverse transcription (RNA to DNA) is a "special transfer" allowed by it. The slogan DNA → RNA → protein is a heuristic (BI.M.H). Regulation covers transcription factors, chromatin state and noncoding

RNA. Epigenetic marks can persist across mitotic divisions. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is a separate, narrower claim and is OPEN in many taxa. - BI.O.A1.3 Transmission. Mendel's laws: segregation holds for a diploid locus under regular meiosis; independent assortment holds only for loci that are unlinked. Linkage is the exception that maps chromosomes. Horizontal gene transfer moves sequence between lineages and breaks a strictly branching tree. Plasmids are its common vehicle in prokaryotes. - BI.O.A1.4 Variation. Mutation is a change in sequence: point, indel, copy-number or chromosomal. Its fitness effect is

a later claim (BI.O.A4), not part of the definition. Recombination generates new allele combinations. The gene has two definitions, molecular (transcribed region) and classical (unit of inheritance); a sentence must say which. Named objects: allele, genotype, phenotype, locus, codon, plasmid, recombination, horizontal transfer, epigenetic mark. ### BI.O.A2 Cell Situation. The cell is the smallest unit that is alive. Complication. Viruses replicate but are not cells, and v1 filed them twice. Membranes and ATP were also filed in chemistry. Question. Which claims about the cell does biology own? Answer. Biology owns

the cell plan, its membrane and excitability, its metabolism as organised chemistry, its division, and the acellular replicators that depend on it. Key line (inductive; plural noun: cell functions; dimension: what part of cell life the claim is about; order: structure, then flux, then reproduction, then dependants). Members (5): Cell plans and origin · Membrane, excitability and signalling · Metabolism · Cycle and division · Acellular replicators. - BI.O.A2.1 Cell plans and origin. Cell theory: organisms are cells or assemblages of cells, and cells arise from cells. It is a

historical generalisation with one stated exception class: the origin of life. Prokaryotic plans (bacteria, archaea) lack a nucleus. Eukaryotic plans have a nucleus and membrane-bounded organelles. Endosymbiosis explains mitochondria and plastids. Origin of life is an OPEN programme; it uses CH.O.A3 and EA.O.A3. - BI.O.A2.2 Membrane, excitability and signalling. A lipid bilayer sets an inside; transport is passive or pumped. The resting membrane potential is owned here. The Nernst equation that gives each ion's equilibrium potential is owned by chemistry (uses CH.O.A3.3). The action potential is owned here as an

excitable-membrane claim. CONTESTED: alternative home MS.O.A2. Signalling covers receptor, second messenger and response. Specificity is binding, not a new force. - BI.O.A2.3 Metabolism. Pathways capture and spend energy. ATP and proton-motive force as cell currency are owned here. ATP coupling as free energy (ΔG) is owned by CH.O.A3 (uses CH.O.A3). Enzyme kinetics, including Michaelis–Menten, is owned by CH.O.A4.2. Michaelis–Menten holds under a quasi-steady-state complex, substrate in excess of enzyme, and no product inhibition (uses CH.O.A4.2). Photosynthesis and aerobic respiration are the two dominant planetary routes. Chemosynthesis (chemolithotrophy) and fermentation are

other major routes. - BI.O.A2.4 Cycle and division. Replication, segregation and division, with checkpoints. Mitosis preserves ploidy. Meiosis halves ploidy and recombines homologues. - BI.O.A2.5 Acellular replicators. Viruses, viroids and similar replicators reproduce only inside a host cell. The Baltimore scheme classifies viruses into seven classes by genome type and route to mRNA. Quasispecies theory describes mutant swarms under high mutation rate; its fit to real viral populations is CONTESTED. Virology as a named group is in the catalog register (BI.B.K). Named objects: cell theory, prokaryote, eukaryote, endosymbiosis, membrane potential,

action potential, ATP, proton-motive force, mitosis, meiosis, Baltimore class. ### BI.O.A3 Organism Situation. One individual integrates cells into a working body. Complication. Medicine restates normal physiology, mind claims behaviour, and agriculture and veterinary science had no home. Question. Which claims about the individual organism does biology own? Answer. Biology owns normal function, development, defence, behaviour of non-human animals, and the organism in production with its disorders. Human disorder is MD. Key line (inductive; plural noun: organismal functions; dimension: what the individual must do or undergo; order: maintain, build, defend, act,

be used). Members (5): Homeostasis and exchange · Development and life history · Immune defence · Behaviour · Production and animal health. - BI.O.A3.1 Homeostasis and exchange. Regulated variables are held in a range by negative feedback; not every internal value is constant. Exchange of gas, water, solute and heat is constrained by surface-to-volume ratio. Circulation and branching relieve that constraint. Chronobiology (circadian and other clocks) is a homeostatic-control claim and lives here. Normal human physiology is owned here; MD.O.A1 cites it. - BI.O.A3.2 Development and life history. Development turns

one cell into a patterned body. Differentiation is change in gene expression under position and history. Morphogen gradients and induction are mechanisms, not universal laws. A stem cell can self-renew and produce differentiated daughters; potency is a measured range. Life history covers growth, reproduction and ageing, with trade-offs as the claim. Evo-devo lives here and cites BI.O.A4. - BI.O.A3.3 Immune defence. Innate and adaptive recognition, and self versus non-self as a functional distinction with known failures. The antibody as a molecule is CH.O.A3; the system is organismal. Normal immune function

is owned here; human immune disorder is MD.O.A1.1. - BI.O.A3.4 Behaviour. Action selected by sensory input and internal state in non-human animals. Ethology and behavioural ecology of individuals live here. Neural circuits and systems are owned by MS.O.A2. Human behaviour is owned by MS.O.A1. - BI.O.A3.5 Production and animal health. The organism kept or grown for use: crop, livestock, aquaculture and forestry organisms. Husbandry claims state the conditions, the population and the measure; no universal yield is owned. Disorder, diagnosis and treatment of non-human animals are owned here. The drug

substance and its residue in human food are owned by MD.O.A4.1 (uses MD.O.A4.1, MD.O.A4.4). The food molecule is CH; a food standard is W12. Plant form (root, shoot, meristem) sits across A3.1–A3.2 at the same level as animal form. Named objects: homeostasis, negative feedback, morphogen, stem cell, potency, circadian clock, innate immunity, adaptive immunity, ethogram, yield, animal disease. ### BI.O.A4 Descent Situation. Lineages change across generations. Complication. Population genetics, quantitative genetics and phylogeny were split across two v1 bridges. Hardy–Weinberg and heritability lacked hypotheses or a cell. Question. Which claims

about change across generations does biology own? Answer. Biology owns the processes that change allele frequencies, the genetics of continuous traits, the splitting of lineages, the pattern of relationship and the pattern above the species. Key line (inductive; plural noun: descent claims; dimension: the resolution of the change; order: within population to above species). Members (5): Population-genetic processes · Quantitative genetics · Speciation · Phylogenetic pattern · Macroevolution. - BI.O.A4.1 Population-genetic processes. Natural selection: heritable variation that affects reproductive success changes allele frequencies. Drift is stronger in small effective populations.

Hardy–Weinberg principle: with no selection, mutation, migration or drift (very large population), and random mating at an autosomal locus with discrete generations, allele frequencies stay constant. Under the same conditions genotype frequencies reach p², 2pq, q² after one generation. Nonrandom mating alone changes genotype frequencies, not allele frequencies. Hardy–Weinberg is a null model, not a mechanism. The Price equation partitions change in a mean trait into selection and transmission terms; it is an identity given defined fitness and trait values. Hamilton's rule (rB > C) holds under its derivation's assumptions,

typically weak selection and additive fitness effects; its generality is CONTESTED. An evolutionarily stable strategy is the MA solution concept applied to fitness payoffs (uses MA.B.C4). Fitness is reproductive success in a stated environment. - BI.O.A4.2 Quantitative genetics. Broad-sense heritability H² = V_G/V_P. Narrow-sense heritability h² = V_A/V_P. Both are variance ratios in a stated population and environment, not individual destinies. The breeder's equation R = h²S holds for a trait under truncation-like selection, with additive effects and no genotype–environment covariance. Human heritability estimates are owned here; MS.O.A3 cites them.

- BI.O.A4.3 Speciation. Lineages cease to exchange genes. Allopatric, parapatric and sympatric routes differ in geography; none is required. Species concepts (biological, phylogenetic, morphological) are naming practice in BI.M.5. - BI.O.A4.4 Phylogenetic pattern. A phylogeny is a hypothesis of relationship. A clade is a common ancestor and all its descendants. Rank (family, order) is a convention (W12). Horizontal transfer and incomplete lineage sorting make gene trees differ from species trees. - BI.O.A4.5 Macroevolution. Pattern above the species, read from phylogeny and fossils. It needs no separate mechanism, though rates and

constraints differ. The organism biology of fossils is owned here; occurrence in a stratum is EA.O.A3. Mass-extinction tempo is a pattern claim shared by citation with EA.O.A3. Named objects: natural selection, drift, Hardy–Weinberg, Price equation, Hamilton's rule, ESS, heritability, breeder's equation, clade, species tree, gene tree. ### BI.O.A5 Ecological interaction Situation. Organisms act on each other and on matter and energy. Complication. Population growth was double-filed with descent; Lotka–Volterra was filed as a method. Biogeography and biogeochemical cycles are claimed by Earth science. Question. Which claims about interaction does biology

own? Answer. Biology owns non-human population dynamics, pairwise interactions, community structure, ecosystem flux and the distribution of life. Key line (inductive; plural noun: interaction claims; dimension: the number of parties and the currency; order: one population to the biosphere). Members (5): Population dynamics · Interactions · Community · Ecosystem flux · Biogeography. - BI.O.A5.1 Population dynamics. Exponential growth dN/dt = rN holds for constant per-capita rate r with unlimited resources and no structure. Logistic growth dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) adds a fixed carrying capacity K and linear density dependence.

K holds only in a stated setting. Human demography is owned by MS.O.A5. - BI.O.A5.2 Interactions. Classified by the sign of the effect on each party: competition (−/−), predation and parasitism (+/−), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), amensalism (−/0), and neutralism (0/0) as the null. The Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations assume a well-mixed system, exponential prey growth without predators, and linear functional responses. The equation is owned here; its simulation is BI.M.4. - BI.O.A5.3 Community. Who co-occurs, and the structure of the interaction web. Diversity is a count or a named index;

say which. Niche is the set of conditions and resources under which a population persists, fundamental versus realised. The host-associated microbiome is a community claim here, citing BI.O.A3 for host function. - BI.O.A5.4 Ecosystem flux. Energy flow and matter cycling through a community plus the abiotic pool. Trophic transfer efficiency measured across ecosystems runs about 5–20 percent (Pauly and Christensen 1995). The 10 percent rule is a heuristic (BI.M.H). Biological carbon and nitrogen fluxes are owned here. CONTESTED: AGU files them in Biogeosciences; alternative home EA.O.A4.3. Water balance is EA.O.A4.2.

- BI.O.A5.5 Biogeography. The spatial distribution of life, set by dispersal, barrier, climate and history. Endemism and disjunction are patterns needing a historical explanation. CONTESTED: alternative EA.O.A4 for the map pattern alone. Island biogeography theory (MacArthur–Wilson) holds under a balance of immigration and extinction depending on isolation and area; its equilibrium assumption is CONTESTED. Named objects: carrying capacity, Lotka–Volterra, niche, diversity index, food web, trophic efficiency, microbiome, endemism, island biogeography.

## 2. Governing thought Earth science (geography and geology) is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Every Earth claim is about one of five questions: Materials · Internal motion · Deep time · Surface and fluid envelopes · Human spatial organization. ## 3. Key line - Logic: inductive. - Plural noun: questions about the Earth. - Dimension: what the claim is about. - Order: structural, from rock to settlement. Members (5): 1. Materials 2. Internal motion 3. Deep time 4. Surface and fluid envelopes

5. Human spatial organization Change from v1. "Surface pattern" becomes "Surface and fluid envelopes". This closes the ownership gap for ocean, atmosphere and cryosphere (audit error 11) without a sixth member. The laws used (fluid dynamics, radiative transfer, thermodynamics) remain PH. The dated Earth state and its circulation are EA. CONTESTED: alternative is a PH cell for climate mechanism with EA citing. Dimension fix. v1 said "what the claim quantifies". Place meaning is not a quantity. The dimension is "what the claim is about" (audit error 5). ## 4. Face

O — Objects ### EA.O.A1 Materials Situation. Minerals, rocks, crustal fluids and soil parent material make up the solid Earth. Complication. Chemistry claims the bond and speciation; v1 defined a mineral too narrowly and gave metamorphic facies a single P–T point. Question. Which claims about Earth materials does EA own? Answer. EA owns identity, assemblage, origin class and distribution of materials in Earth reservoirs. Speciation chemistry is CH. Key line (inductive; plural noun: material classes; dimension: the origin or state of the material; order: crystal to fluid). Members (5): Minerals

· Igneous rocks · Sedimentary rocks · Metamorphic rocks · Crustal fluids and element distribution. - EA.O.A1.1 Minerals. IMA definition: a mineral is an element or compound, normally crystalline, formed by geological processes (Nickel 1995). Its composition is definite but not necessarily fixed, allowing solid solution. Silicates dominate the crust. Identification is by habit, cleavage, hardness, optics, XRD and microprobe. Names follow IMA (W12). - EA.O.A1.2 Igneous rocks. Formed from melt. Texture records cooling rate. Bowen's reaction series is the idealised crystallisation order of a basaltic melt cooling slowly with

equilibrium reaction. Few magmas complete it. Classification follows IUGS (W12). - EA.O.A1.3 Sedimentary rocks. Formed by deposition and lithification. Grain size, sorting and composition are the descriptors. A sedimentary structure (cross-bed, ripple, graded bed) is evidence of the depositing process. Sedimentology is the A1 process claim; the sequence is EA.O.A3. - EA.O.A1.4 Metamorphic rocks. Formed by solid-state change. A metamorphic facies (Eskola 1920) is a set of mineral assemblages formed over a stated range of pressure and temperature. Foliation records directed stress. The rock cycle is a path among A1.2–A1.4,

not a clock. - EA.O.A1.5 Crustal fluids and element distribution. Groundwater, brines, hydrothermal fluids and melts in the crust. Element distribution in Earth reservoirs (geochemistry as distribution) is owned here. Speciation and reaction in a natural matrix is CH (uses CH, environmental chemistry cell). Soil parent material is here; the soil body is EA.O.A4.4. Named objects: mineral, solid solution, Bowen's series, facies, foliation, cross-bed, rock cycle, ore deposit (application instance), hydrothermal fluid. ### EA.O.A2 Internal motion Situation. Heat and gravity drive motion in the interior and lithosphere. Complication. v1 said

"magnitude is energy", stated isostasy imprecisely, and left the geodynamo and geodesy unplaced. Question. Which claims about how the Earth moves inside does EA own? Answer. EA owns plate kinematics, deformation, interior structure and fields, isostatic support, and magmatism. Wave and elasticity laws are PH. Key line (inductive; plural noun: motion claims; dimension: what moves and at what depth; order: surface plates to deep interior and back to melt). Members (5): Plate kinematics · Deformation · Interior structure and fields · Isostasy and flexure · Magmatism. - EA.O.A2.1 Plate kinematics.

The lithosphere is divided into plates that move relative to one another. Boundaries are divergent, convergent or transform. Evidence: continental fit, rock and fossil correlation, seafloor magnetic anomalies, seismicity, and geodetic motion. Euler-pole description of plate motion holds for rigid plates on a sphere. - EA.O.A2.2 Deformation. Stress and strain in rock. Brittle faulting dominates near the surface; ductile flow dominates at depth. A fold is geometry; a fault is a fracture with offset. Earthquake size: magnitude is a logarithmic measure. Moment magnitude Mw derives from seismic moment M₀ =

μAD (rigidity, rupture area, mean slip). Radiated energy rises about 32 times per unit magnitude. Intensity is felt effect (USGS, cited in audit). - EA.O.A2.3 Interior structure and fields. Seismology infers layering from travel times. S waves do not pass through the outer core, which is evidence it is liquid. The geodynamo (the field generated in the liquid outer core) is owned here as an Earth-state claim. The MHD equations used are PH. Geodesy as a claim — figure of the Earth, gravity field — is owned here. - EA.O.A2.4

Isostasy and flexure. The lithosphere is in buoyant equilibrium on the asthenosphere. Airy compensation uses crustal roots; Pratt compensation uses lateral density change. Many ranges are partly supported by flexure of an elastic plate. Glacial isostatic adjustment is the observable rebound after ice load. - EA.O.A2.5 Magmatism. Melt generation at ridges (decompression), subduction zones (flux melting) and hotspots. A hotspot track is evidence of plate motion over a source, interpreted, not seen. Volcanic eruption as a hazard event enters EA.O.A5.5. Named objects: plate, Euler pole, transform fault, moment magnitude, seismic

moment, outer core, geodynamo, geoid, Airy and Pratt isostasy, flexure, hotspot. ### EA.O.A3 Deep time Situation. The record orders and ages events across 4.5 billion years. Complication. v1 said all time-scale boundaries are reference sections, misattributed Steno's rules and filed uniformitarianism twice. Question. Which claims about the sequence and age of Earth events does EA own? Answer. EA owns relative order, correlation, numeric age, the time-scale convention and the occurrence of life in the record. The decay law is PH. Key line (inductive; plural noun: time claims; dimension: how the

time is established; order: relative before numeric before convention). Members (5): Relative order · Correlation · Numeric age · Time-scale convention · Record of life and climate. - EA.O.A3.1 Relative order. Steno (1669) gave superposition, original horizontality and lateral continuity. Superposition holds for undisturbed, non-overturned layered sequences. Cross-cutting relations are credited to Steno and Hutton. The principle of inclusions is Lyell's. An unconformity is evidence of missing time. - EA.O.A3.2 Correlation. Matching strata between places by fossils, lithology, magnetic polarity, stable isotopes or tephra. An index fossil is widespread, short-lived

and distinctive. A polarity reversal is a time marker, not a cause. - EA.O.A3.3 Numeric age. The decay law N = N₀e^(−λt) is owned by PH (uses PH nuclear cell). The dating claim is owned here. It holds when the system closed at a stated time, with known initial daughter and no later gain or loss. Carbon-14 serves late-Quaternary organic matter, to about 50,000 years. U–Pb and other systems serve deep time. Luminescence, dendrochronology and varves are other numeric methods. - EA.O.A3.4 Time-scale convention. The ICS chart divides eon, era,

period, epoch and age. Phanerozoic and Ediacaran boundaries are GSSPs (reference sections). Most Precambrian boundaries are GSSAs, numeric ages such as 2500 Ma for Archean–Proterozoic. Warrant W12. - EA.O.A3.5 Record of life and climate. Occurrence of organisms in strata is owned here; their biology is BI.O.A4.5. Mass extinctions are pattern claims about that record. Paleoclimate and paleoceanography as dated states, read from proxies, are owned here. Their mechanism cites EA.O.A4.3. The Anthropocene as a formal unit was rejected by the IUGS in March 2024 (stratigraphy.org/news/152). Named objects: superposition, unconformity, index

fossil, polarity chron, closure temperature, U–Pb, GSSP, GSSA, proxy record. ### EA.O.A4 Surface and fluid envelopes Situation. Land, water, air, ice and soil are arranged and circulate at and above the surface now. Complication. Atmosphere, ocean and cryosphere had no owner; Darcy's law lacked hypotheses; hydrogeology sat in two halves. Question. Which claims about the present surface and its fluid envelopes does EA own? Answer. EA owns landforms and process, water on and under land, the atmosphere–ocean–climate state and circulation, the cryosphere, and the soil body. Key line (inductive; plural

noun: surface and envelope claims; dimension: which part of the surface system the claim is about; order: solid surface outward then back to the skin). Members (5): Landforms and process · Water on and under land · Atmosphere, ocean and climate · Cryosphere · Soil. - EA.O.A4.1 Landforms and process. Geomorphology: landforms as products of rock, climate and time. Processes are weathering, mass wasting, fluvial, glacial, aeolian and coastal. A graded river adjusts slope and channel to its water and sediment load. The adjustment is a tendency, not a guarantee.

Uniformitarianism is a methodological premise in EA.M.H, cited here. - EA.O.A4.2 Water on and under land. Water balance for a drainage basin over a period: P = ET + Q + ΔS (precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, storage change). Groundwater and aquifer claims (transmissivity, storativity) are owned here. Darcy's law q = −K∇h holds for laminar flow (Reynolds number below about 1–10) in a saturated, rigid porous medium. Its owner is EN transport closure (uses EN.O.A2); CONTESTED, alternative PH continuum. The well is EN. - EA.O.A4.3 Atmosphere, ocean and climate. Climate is

the statistics of weather over a stated period, typically 30 years (WMO). Its state, circulation and change as a dated Earth claim are owned here. Controls are latitude, altitude, continentality, ocean currents and circulation. The governing laws (Navier–Stokes, radiative transfer, thermodynamics) are PH. Ocean circulation, sea level and marine biogeochemical state are owned here; marine biology is BI.O.A5. Köppen–Geiger is a classification (W12), not a mechanism. Climate change attribution claims owe W2 and W5. Atmospheric electricity and the upper atmosphere are refused to PH (space physics). - EA.O.A4.4 Cryosphere. Glaciers,

ice sheets, sea ice, permafrost and snow as surface mass. Mass balance (accumulation minus ablation) is the core claim. Glacier flow by Glen's flow law assumes power-law creep of polycrystalline ice with exponent near 3 (UNVERIFIED exponent range). Glacial landforms are EA.O.A4.1. - EA.O.A4.5 Soil. The soil body: weathered parent material plus organic matter, organised in horizons. Pedology owns the profile here. Soil mechanics (effective stress, Mohr–Coulomb) is EN. Soil chemistry is CH. Soil biota are BI.O.A5.3. Named objects: drainage basin, base level, water balance, aquifer, Darcy's law, climate normal,

thermohaline circulation, mass balance, permafrost, soil horizon, Köppen–Geiger class. ### EA.O.A5 Human spatial organization Situation. People locate, move, and make places and regions under constraint. Complication. v1 filed distance decay three ways, defined vulnerability wrongly, gave hazard and risk no cell, and had no home for coupled human–natural systems. Question. Which claims about the spatial organisation of people does EA own? Answer. EA owns location and interaction, region and place, economic and urban pattern, political space, and nature–society with risk. Key line (inductive; plural noun: spatial-organisation claims; dimension: what organises

the pattern; order: distance, then meaning, then market, then authority, then nature). Members (5): Location and interaction · Region and place · Economic and urban pattern · Political space · Nature–society and risk. - EA.O.A5.1 Location and interaction. Site and situation; absolute and relative location. Distance decay is the claim that interaction falls with distance, modified by origin and destination size. It is owned here. Gravity-model estimation is EA.M.5. In trade, the gravity equation has structural derivations (Anderson 1979; Anderson and van Wincoop 2003); that derivation is EC. In migration,

gravity models are mostly reduced-form. CONTESTED for migration. - EA.O.A5.2 Region and place. A region is a delimited area of stated similarity (formal), flow (functional) or perception (perceptual). Place is a location invested with meaning; its warrant is W8. Area studies as a catalog of regions is refused (sector, not a cell). - EA.O.A5.3 Economic and urban pattern. Where production and exchange happen. Central place theory predicts a hexagonal hierarchy on an isotropic plain with uniform population and transport, and rational, nearest-centre consumers. The spatial pattern is owned here. Bid-rent

as allocation is EC. Urban models (concentric, sector, multiple nuclei) are ideal types. - EA.O.A5.4 Political space. Territory and boundary as spatial claims. A boundary is a claim enforced, not a natural line. The authority behind it is PO. Its legal validity is LA. - EA.O.A5.5 Nature–society and risk. Coupled human–natural systems: pressure, state, impact and response, under a stated boundary. This absorbs environmental science claims (Grok "EV"). Risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability (IPCC AR6 WGII glossary). Vulnerability is the propensity to be adversely affected: sensitivity plus lack

of capacity to cope and adapt. Exposure is a separate factor. The hazard cites EA.O.A2 or A4. Policy is PO; price is EC; duty is LA. Population counts are MS.O.A5. Named objects: site, situation, distance decay, formal region, place, central place, bid-rent pattern, boundary, territory, hazard, exposure, vulnerability, risk. Pattison (1964) mapping, corrected. Spatial tradition → A5.1 and the map pattern of A4. Earth-science tradition → A1–A4. Man–land tradition → A5.5. Area-studies tradition → refused as a catalog of regions.

## 2. Governing thought Medicine is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five clinical questions: disorders, causes and mechanisms, diagnosis and prognosis, treatment and drugs, and populations and prevention. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the clinical question asked of a disorder.** Logic inductive. Order: the clinical sequence. 1. Disorders 2. Causes and mechanisms 3. Diagnosis and prognosis 4. Treatment and drugs 5. Populations and prevention **MECE test.** "Type 2 diabetes is defined by HbA1c ≥ 48 mmol/mol" is A1 (a

classification rule, W12). "Insulin resistance drives it" is A2. "HbA1c has sensitivity s" is A3. "Metformin lowers HbA1c" is A4. "Prevalence is rising" is A5. ## 4. Face O — Objects ### MD.O.A1 Disorders **SCQA.** Situation. Medicine first names what is wrong. Names come from classification rules, which are conventions, but the entities they name are meant to be real. Complication. The same suffering can be cut into entities in more than one way, and thresholds move with evidence and committee decisions. Some names pick out a cause, some a

mechanism, and some only a cluster of signs. Question. What is a disorder, and which kinds of claim about disorders does medicine own? Answer. Medicine owns the working definition of a disorder, the classification systems that name disorders, the diagnosis of mental disorder, and the clinical handling of clustered and co-occurring conditions. The concept of disease in general is argued in PL (uses PL.O.A4). **Key line.** Inductive. Plural noun: kinds of disorder claim. Dimension: how the disorder is individuated. Order: from the single entity, to the system that names it,

to the hardest case, to combinations. Members (4): Disease entities · Classification · Mental disorder · Syndromes and multimorbidity. - **MD.O.A1.1 Disease entities.** A disorder is a departure from normal function that harms the person. Normal function is owned by BI (uses BI.O.A3.1). The concept itself is debated in PL; MD uses a working definition. - MD.O.A1.1.1 Immune disorders: autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, allergy. Normal immune function is BI (uses BI.O.A3.3). - MD.O.A1.1.2 Neoplasms: the clinical entity is here; the cell biology is BI. - MD.O.A1.1.3 A disease entity is individuated by

at least one of aetiology, mechanism or clinical picture. A specialist can test which of the three a given name rests on. - MD.O.A1.1.4 Harm is part of the working definition. A biological variant without harm, such as a benign anatomical variant, is not a disorder here. - **MD.O.A1.2 Classification.** Disorders are named by published systems, ICD-11 (in effect from 1 January 2022) and DSM-5-TR (2022). Classification rules are W12. - MD.O.A1.2.1 Diagnostic thresholds, such as HbA1c for diabetes, are conventions set by expert bodies. - MD.O.A1.2.2 A change in

a threshold changes measured prevalence without any change in the population. Prevalence trends across a threshold change are therefore not comparable without adjustment. - MD.O.A1.2.3 Inter-rater reliability, usually reported as Cohen's kappa, is a property of a diagnostic category in a stated setting. It is measured in field trials, not assumed from the text of the criteria. - **MD.O.A1.3 Mental disorder.** The diagnosis is MD; normal cognition is MS (uses MS.O.A1); the concept of mental disorder is PL (CONTESTED). - MD.O.A1.3.1 Categorical against dimensional models (RDoC, HiTOP) as competing classification

programmes. - MD.O.A1.3.2 Most DSM categories are defined by symptom criteria, not by a known biological marker. A claim that a biomarker defines a psychiatric category is OPEN for most categories. - MD.O.A1.3.3 Comorbidity between psychiatric categories is common. Under the dimensional programme it is read as shared underlying dimensions (CONTESTED). - **MD.O.A1.4 Syndromes and multimorbidity.** Co-occurring conditions and frailty are handled as clinical objects in their own right. - MD.O.A1.4.1 A syndrome is a recurring cluster of signs and symptoms whose single cause is unknown or not required. When

a cause is found, the syndrome may be renamed as a disease entity (A1.1). - MD.O.A1.4.2 Multimorbidity, two or more chronic conditions in one person, rises with age. Trials often exclude such patients, so single-disease evidence transfers to them with stated uncertainty. Named objects: disease entity, syndrome, ICD-11, DSM-5-TR, diagnostic threshold, inter-rater reliability (kappa; hypothesis: raters classify independently), RDoC, HiTOP, multimorbidity, frailty. ### MD.O.A2 Causes and mechanisms **SCQA.** Situation. Every disorder invites the question why it occurs. Causes range from pathogens to genes to social conditions. Complication. Evidence for causation

is often observational, causes interact, and a mechanism shown in cells may not operate in patients. Question. Which causal claims does medicine own, and what warrant does each need? Answer. Medicine owns pathogen causation, genetic causation of disease, the pathophysiology of disordered processes, and the effect of environmental and social exposures on disease. The underlying evolutionary, cellular and social processes are owned elsewhere and cited. **Key line.** Inductive. Plural noun: kinds of cause. Dimension: where the cause originates. Order: from outside agent, to inherited make-up, to internal process, to surroundings.

Members (4): Pathogens · Genetic causes · Pathophysiology · Environmental and social determinants. - **MD.O.A2.1 Pathogens.** Germ theory holds that specific microorganisms cause specific infectious diseases. Koch's postulates are a historical heuristic, not a test for all pathogens (asymptomatic carriers and unculturable agents fail them). - MD.O.A2.1.1 Antimicrobial resistance: selection under drug exposure (the evolutionary mechanism is BI, uses BI.O.A4.1). - MD.O.A2.1.2 Molecular criteria, based on finding pathogen nucleic acid in diseased tissue, extend causal attribution to unculturable agents. Detection of nucleic acid alone does not show a viable or

causal agent. - MD.O.A2.1.3 Host factors change the outcome of exposure to the same agent. The pathogen is necessary for an infectious disease but often not sufficient. - **MD.O.A2.2 Genetic causes.** Monogenic disorders follow Mendelian inheritance; polygenic risk scores sum many small effects, and their predictive power varies by ancestry. - MD.O.A2.2.1 Penetrance, the fraction of carriers who develop the disorder, is often below one. Recurrence risks from pedigrees state the penetrance assumed. - MD.O.A2.2.2 A polygenic score built in one ancestry group usually predicts less well in others. Transportability

across ancestries is OPEN. - MD.O.A2.2.3 Mendelian randomisation uses genetic variants as instruments for an exposure. Hypotheses: the variant affects the exposure, has no path to the outcome except through it, and shares no confounder with the outcome. - **MD.O.A2.3 Pathophysiology.** Medicine owns the mechanism of a disordered process, such as atherosclerosis or insulin resistance. The normal process it departs from is BI. - MD.O.A2.3.1 A mechanism shown in cells or animals is a hypothesis about patients until shown in human data. Failure to transfer is a known defeater. -

MD.O.A2.3.2 Many chronic disorders arise from several interacting mechanisms. A single-mechanism account of Alzheimer's disease, such as the amyloid hypothesis, is CONTESTED. - **MD.O.A2.4 Environmental and social determinants.** Exposures such as tobacco and air pollution, and deprivation, change disease risk. The social structure is MS (uses MS.O.A5); the exposure source is EV. - MD.O.A2.4.1 The link between smoking and lung cancer is a model case of causal inference from observational data. It rests on consistency, strength, dose–response and temporality across many studies. - MD.O.A2.4.2 Socioeconomic gradients in health hold across

many conditions. The size of the gradient is stated for a named population and measure of deprivation. - MD.O.A2.4.3 Exposure–response functions for air pollutants are estimated in named cohorts. Extrapolation below the lowest observed level is a stated assumption. Named objects: germ theory, Koch's postulates (hypotheses: agent isolable and culturable; one agent per disease; a susceptible host can be tested), antimicrobial resistance, penetrance, polygenic risk score, Mendelian randomisation (hypotheses in A2.2.3), atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, amyloid hypothesis, social gradient, exposure–response function, Bradford Hill viewpoints (guides, not tests). ### MD.O.A3 Diagnosis and

prognosis **SCQA.** Situation. Before treating, a clinician must recognise the disorder and estimate its course. Complication. Tests are imperfect, and their value depends on who is tested. Prognostic models built in one place often fail elsewhere. Question. Which claims about recognising a disorder and forecasting its course does medicine own? Answer. Medicine owns the use of signs and tests, the accuracy of tests in populations, prognosis and its models, and tests applied to people without symptoms. The mathematics of probability is owned by MA.O.A5. **Key line.** Inductive. Plural noun: kinds

of recognition and forecast. Dimension: what the clinician learns from the information. Order: gather, weigh, forecast, then extend to the well. Members (4): Signs, symptoms and tests · Test accuracy · Prognosis · Screening tests. - **MD.O.A3.1 Signs, symptoms and tests.** Clinical examination, imaging and laboratory tests are the sources of diagnostic information. - MD.O.A3.1.1 History taking supplies much of the information used in many primary-care diagnoses. The proportion varies by setting and is stated per study (UNVERIFIED as a general figure). - MD.O.A3.1.2 Laboratory reference intervals are usually the

central 95 per cent of a healthy reference population. By construction about one healthy person in twenty falls outside a single interval. - **MD.O.A3.2 Test accuracy.** Sensitivity and specificity describe a test against a reference standard. Predictive values depend on prevalence (Bayes' theorem, owned by MA.O.A5). - MD.O.A3.2.1 Likelihood ratios combine with pre-test odds to give post-test odds, assuming test independence. - MD.O.A3.2.2 A receiver operating characteristic curve shows sensitivity against one minus specificity across cut-offs. Choosing a cut-off is a decision about the cost of each error, not a

property of the test. - MD.O.A3.2.3 Spectrum bias arises when accuracy is measured in very sick cases and healthy controls. Such studies overstate accuracy in practice populations. - **MD.O.A3.3 Prognosis.** Survival, course and prognostic models are stated for a named population. A model's calibration and discrimination are stated in that population. - MD.O.A3.3.1 The Kaplan–Meier estimator gives survival over time. Hypothesis: censoring is unrelated to outcome. - MD.O.A3.3.2 A model with good discrimination can be poorly calibrated in a new setting. External validation and recalibration are needed before local use.

- MD.O.A3.3.3 Cancer staging, such as TNM, is a prognostic classification. Its rules are W12; its prognostic value is an empirical claim here. - **MD.O.A3.4 Screening tests.** Testing people without symptoms is a diagnostic act. The programme decision is A5.3. - MD.O.A3.4.1 At low prevalence, even a highly specific test yields many false positives relative to true positives. This follows from Bayes' theorem (uses MA.O.A5). - MD.O.A3.4.2 Overdiagnosis is the detection of disease that would never have caused harm. It is estimated from excess incidence in screened groups, under stated

assumptions about lead time. Named objects: sensitivity, specificity, predictive value, likelihood ratio (hypothesis: conditional independence of tests), ROC curve (hypothesis: reference standard classifies all participants), reference interval, Kaplan–Meier estimator (hypothesis: non-informative censoring), TNM staging, calibration, discrimination, overdiagnosis, STARD. ### MD.O.A4 Treatment and drugs **SCQA.** Situation. Medicine aims to change the course of a disorder. Drugs, procedures and therapies are tested in trials, approved by regulators and monitored after approval. Complication. Effects measured in trials may not hold for the patient in front of the clinician. Surrogate endpoints can mislead, and

harms appear late. Question. Which claims about treatment effect and safety does medicine own? Answer. Medicine owns drug action in patients, procedural and psychological treatments, drug safety, and the evidential stages of drug development. The molecule is CH and the legal authority is LA. **Key line.** Inductive. Plural noun: kinds of intervention claim. Dimension: the means of intervention and its evidential stage. Order: drug action, physical procedure, talking and rehabilitative therapy, then harms and the pathway to approval. Members (5): Pharmacology · Surgery and procedures · Psychological and rehabilitative therapy

· Drug safety · Drug development and regulation. - **MD.O.A4.1 Pharmacology.** Pharmacokinetics covers absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics covers dose–response. The molecule is CH (uses CH.O.A3). - MD.O.A4.1.1 First-order elimination: half-life t½ = ln 2 / k, for linear kinetics. - MD.O.A4.1.2 Therapeutic index as the ratio of toxic to effective dose. - MD.O.A4.1.3 Pharmacogenomics: genotype-dependent drug response. - MD.O.A4.1.4 The Hill dose–response model fits effect as a saturating function of concentration. Hypotheses: reversible binding at equilibrium and one receptor population. - **MD.O.A4.2 Surgery and procedures.** Operations and procedures

change anatomy or physiology by physical means. Their effects are claims of the same kind as drug effects. - MD.O.A4.2.1 Surgical outcomes depend on operator and centre volume for many procedures. The volume–outcome relation is stated per procedure. - MD.O.A4.2.2 Sham-controlled trials are possible for some procedures. Where they exist, they can show smaller effects than unblinded comparisons. - **MD.O.A4.3 Psychological and rehabilitative therapy.** Cognitive behavioural therapy and physiotherapy are treatments tested like others. The mental mechanism is MS. - MD.O.A4.3.1 Blinding of patients is rarely possible in psychological therapy.

Expectancy effects are a stated defeater for effect sizes. - MD.O.A4.3.2 Rehabilitation outcomes are measured as function and participation, not only as disease markers. The measure is named with the claim. - **MD.O.A4.4 Drug safety.** Adverse effects are identified before and after approval. Pharmacovigilance continues after approval. - MD.O.A4.4.1 Residues of veterinary drugs in human food: the safety limit is MD; the animal treatment is AG. - MD.O.A4.4.2 Rare adverse effects are often undetectable in pre-approval trials. By the rule of three, zero events in n patients gives an approximate

95 per cent upper bound of 3/n (uses MA.O.A5). - MD.O.A4.4.3 Spontaneous reporting systems detect signals, not rates. A signal needs a comparative study before a causal claim. - **MD.O.A4.5 Drug development and regulation.** Trials run in phases I–IV; approval comes from bodies such as Medsafe (NZ), the FDA and EMA. The legal authority is LA. - MD.O.A4.5.1 Phase I establishes safety and dose, phase II early efficacy, phase III confirmatory efficacy, and phase IV post-approval effects. - MD.O.A4.5.2 Effects on a surrogate endpoint do not guarantee effects on patient

outcomes. Antiarrhythmic drugs that suppressed arrhythmia yet raised mortality are a known case (CAST). - MD.O.A4.5.3 The randomised controlled trial estimates the average effect of a treatment. Hypotheses: random concealed allocation, adequate power and intention-to-treat analysis. Named objects: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, half-life (hypothesis: first-order kinetics), therapeutic index, Hill model (hypotheses in A4.1.4), pharmacogenomics, sham control, pharmacovigilance, rule of three (hypothesis: independent patients, zero events), surrogate endpoint, trial phases, randomised controlled trial (hypotheses in A4.5.3), number needed to treat (hypothesis: baseline risk matches the patient group), CONSORT. ### MD.O.A5 Populations and prevention

**SCQA.** Situation. Disorders occur in populations, and many are prevented rather than treated. Complication. Population claims rest on surveillance and study design, and an average effect may not hold for subgroups. Transmission models depend on contact assumptions that rarely hold exactly. Question. Which claims about disorders in populations and their prevention does medicine own? Answer. Medicine owns the measurement of disease frequency, the dynamics of transmission, the effect of prevention and screening programmes, the performance of health systems, and the health of named populations. Price, law and policy are owned

elsewhere. **Key line.** Inductive. Plural noun: kinds of population claim. Dimension: what is measured or changed at population level. Order: measure, spread, prevent, deliver, then distribute. Members (5): Epidemiology · Transmission · Prevention and screening programmes · Health systems · Global and Māori health. - **MD.O.A5.1 Epidemiology.** Disease frequency is measured as incidence and prevalence; association as relative and absolute risk. - MD.O.A5.1.1 Prevalence approximates incidence times mean duration in a steady state with low prevalence. The approximation fails when either assumption fails. - MD.O.A5.1.2 Relative risk alone does not

convey benefit. The same relative risk reduction gives a smaller absolute reduction at lower baseline risk. - MD.O.A5.1.3 Direct age standardisation compares rates across populations of different age structure. Hypothesis: a chosen standard population and stable age-specific rates. - **MD.O.A5.2 Transmission.** R0 holds for a fully susceptible population under a stated contact model. The herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R0 assumes homogeneous mixing. - MD.O.A5.2.1 The SIR compartmental model describes susceptible, infected and recovered fractions. Hypotheses: homogeneous mixing, fixed rates and lasting immunity (uses MA.O.A4). - MD.O.A5.2.2 The effective reproduction number

Rt falls as immunity rises and contacts change. An epidemic declines while Rt stays below one. - MD.O.A5.2.3 Heterogeneous contact can lower the herd-immunity threshold below 1 − 1/R0. The size of the reduction depends on the contact structure assumed. - **MD.O.A5.3 Prevention and screening programmes.** Vaccines and screening prevent disease or its harm at population level. Lead-time and length bias are stated defeaters for screening benefit. - MD.O.A5.3.1 Vaccine efficacy is measured in trials; vaccine effectiveness is measured in routine use. The two can differ through population, strain and

waning. - MD.O.A5.3.2 Screening benefit is shown by reduced disease-specific or all-cause mortality in a randomised comparison. Longer survival from diagnosis alone does not show benefit. - MD.O.A5.3.3 Programme criteria, such as those of Wilson and Jungner, are guides to whether screening is worthwhile. They are judgements, not tests. - **MD.O.A5.4 Health systems.** Medicine owns claims about delivery, access and quality of care. Price and finance are EC; law is LA; policy is PO. - MD.O.A5.4.1 The Donabedian framework assesses quality by structure, process and outcome. Hypothesis: the process measured

is linked to the outcome. - MD.O.A5.4.2 Comparisons of providers need risk adjustment for patient mix. Small case numbers make rankings unstable. - **MD.O.A5.5 Global and Māori health.** Health inequities by population. Under the two-mode rule, the tradition-internal side of rongoā and hauora is IK. Its clinical efficacy for a named condition is MD under W3. - MD.O.A5.5.1 Inequity is stated as an absolute and a relative gap in a named measure, such as life expectancy or a disease rate. The two can move in opposite directions. - MD.O.A5.5.2 Differences

in access, quality and outcome of care between population groups are measured with risk adjustment. Unadjusted gaps mix need with quality of care. Named objects: incidence, prevalence, relative risk, absolute risk, age standardisation, R0, Rt, herd-immunity threshold (hypothesis: homogeneous mixing), SIR model (hypotheses in A5.2.1), vaccine efficacy, vaccine effectiveness, lead-time bias, length bias, Wilson–Jungner criteria, Donabedian framework, risk adjustment.

## 2. Governing thought Engineering is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its object claims divide into five balances: force and deformation, mass and momentum, energy and entropy, electromagnetic state, and composition and microstructure. ## 3. Key line This is the key line of Face O, the claim partition of the pyramid. - Logic: inductive. - Plural noun: balances. - Dimension: the quantity whose balance or constitutive closure finishes the predictive model of an artefact. - Order: structural, from load path to material. -

Members (5): 1. force and deformation 2. mass and momentum 3. energy and entropy 4. electromagnetic state 5. composition and microstructure Test for a new member (repairs audit EN #18). A sixth balance is warranted only if an artefact model needs a closing quantity none of the five carries. Information state passes that test and is therefore not an EN balance: it is owned by CS (uses CS.O.A2.4). Failure probability also passes it, and is owned by MA (uses MA.O.A5). Neither is held in EN by fiat. ## 4. Face

O — Objects Face O holds predictive claims used to size or exonerate an artefact. A formula that predicts behaviour lives here, never on Face M (audit EN #6). A law owned elsewhere appears as "uses <owner>"; EN owns the engineering reduction, correlation or closure. ### EN.O.A1 Force and deformation Situation. Structures and machine elements are sized by equilibrium of force and moment, closed by a constitutive law. Complication. v1 divided this cell by "scale", yet listed inertia, which is not a scale (audit EN #5). Question. Which idealisations exhaust

force-and-deformation models? Key line. Plural noun: idealisations. Dimension: what the model idealises the body as. Order: from fewest to most degrees of freedom retained. Members (4): rigid bodies; slender members; deformable continua; contact interfaces. - **EN.O.A1.1 Rigid bodies.** Statics: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 when inertia is negligible. Dynamics: ΣF = m a and ΣM = dH/dt about the centre of mass or a fixed point. These laws are Newtonian mechanics (uses PH.O.A1.1). EN owns the free-body reduction and determinacy check. - EN.O.A1.1.1 Free-body diagram and static determinacy.

- EN.O.A1.1.2 Rigid-body dynamics of mechanisms (linkages, gears, cams). - EN.O.A1.1.3 Lumped vibration models: single- and multi-degree-of-freedom systems with linear springs and viscous damping. Natural frequency ωn = √(k/m) for an undamped linear oscillator. - **EN.O.A1.2 Slender members.** A member whose length greatly exceeds its section is reduced to section resultants plus a kinematic assumption. - EN.O.A1.2.1 Euler–Bernoulli beam. For a prismatic, linear-elastic member with small slopes and plane sections remaining plane and normal: EI d²v/dx² = M(x). With load q positive downward, dM/dx = V and dV/dx = −q

(Gere and Goodno, §4.5; sign convention stated, audit fact check). - EN.O.A1.2.2 Timoshenko beam: adds shear deformation and rotary inertia for deep or short beams. - EN.O.A1.2.3 Torsion of a circular shaft. For a linear-elastic, circular or annular, prismatic bar under small twist: T = G J θ / L and τ = T r / J. - EN.O.A1.2.4 Euler column buckling. For an initially straight, slender, linear-elastic, centrally loaded column: Pcr = π² E I / (K L)². Stocky columns leave this formula for a tangent-modulus or code curve.

- EN.O.A1.2.5 Kirchhoff–Love plate and Mindlin–Reissner plate. Kirchhoff–Love applies to thin plates with normals staying normal; Mindlin–Reissner admits transverse shear for moderately thick plates. - EN.O.A1.2.6 Thin-walled pressure vessel. For wall thickness much less than radius, under internal pressure p: hoop stress pr/t and longitudinal stress pr/2t. - **EN.O.A1.3 Deformable continua.** The parent theory when section assumptions fail. - EN.O.A1.3.1 Cauchy stress and traction t = σᵀn (uses PH.O.A1.5 for the continuum balance laws). - EN.O.A1.3.2 Isotropic linear elasticity (Hooke). For small strain, a linear, isotropic material: σ = λ

tr(ε) I + 2μ ε, with G = E / 2(1+ν). Uses PH.O.A1.5. - EN.O.A1.3.3 Yield criteria: Tresca (maximum shear) and von Mises (distortion energy), for isotropic ductile metals under quasi-static load. - EN.O.A1.3.4 Mohr's circle: principal stresses and maximum shear from the plane-stress transformation. - EN.O.A1.3.5 Linear-elastic fracture mechanics. Under small-scale yielding, K = Y σ √(π a). Mode I, plane-strain failure occurs when K reaches KIc (ASTM E399). - EN.O.A1.3.6 Fatigue life. Basquin (stress-life) and Coffin–Manson (strain-life) relations, fitted per material. Paris law da/dN = C (ΔK)^m holds

in region II only; C and m depend on material and R-ratio (Paris and Erdogan 1963). - EN.O.A1.3.7 Geomechanics. Terzaghi effective stress σ′ = σ − u for saturated soil. Mohr–Coulomb strength τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ for drained soil and rock joints. CONTESTED: EA.O.A1 (rock and soil as earth materials) is the alternative owner; EN keeps the strength closure, EA owns genesis. - **EN.O.A1.4 Contact interfaces.** - EN.O.A1.4.1 Hertz contact. For two smooth, elastic, non-conforming bodies with frictionless contact and small contact area: contact radius and peak

pressure follow from load, curvatures and moduli. CONTESTED: PH.O.A1.5 is the alternative owner. - EN.O.A1.4.2 Coulomb friction: tangential force bounded by μ times normal force, an empirical closure. - EN.O.A1.4.3 Archard wear law: worn volume proportional to load times sliding distance over hardness, with a fitted wear coefficient (UNVERIFIED as to standard notation). - EN.O.A1.4.4 Concepts: stress concentration, Saint-Venant decay, shear centre, slenderness, ductility, redundancy, mechanism. Miner's rule (linear damage sum) is not a Face O claim. It sits in the heuristics register EN.H. ### EN.O.A2 Mass and momentum Situation.

A flow is closed by conservation of mass and momentum plus a constitutive relation for fluid stress. Complication. v1 had no key line here (audit EN #12), and filed Navier–Stokes, Bernoulli and Reynolds number in both PH and EN. Question. Which flow domains exhaust mass-and-momentum models in engineering? Key line. Plural noun: flow domains. Dimension: the boundary that confines the flow. Order: from fully confined to unconfined medium. Members (5): internal flows; external flows; free-surface flows; compressible and acoustic flows; porous-medium flows. Shared basis. Integral mass and momentum balances on

a control volume, and the Navier–Stokes equations for a Newtonian fluid, are owned by physics (uses PH.O.A1.5). Existence and regularity of Navier–Stokes solutions is MA (uses MA.O.A4). EN owns the reductions below. - **EN.O.A2.1 Internal flows.** - EN.O.A2.1.1 Bernoulli equation along a streamline, for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow: p/ρ + V²/2 + g z = constant. Uses PH.O.A1.5. A loss term is added, not derived, when the hypotheses fail. - EN.O.A2.1.2 Darcy–Weisbach head loss h_f = f (L/D) V²/2g, where f is the Darcy (Moody) friction factor, four times the

Fanning factor. - EN.O.A2.1.3 Colebrook equation and Moody chart for f in fully developed turbulent pipe flow (empirical closure). Minor losses K V²/2g. - EN.O.A2.1.4 Pump and fan matching: head-capacity curve against system curve. Affinity laws hold only between dynamically similar operating points. - EN.O.A2.1.5 Reynolds lubrication equation, for thin, viscous, laminar films with negligible inertia (tribology). - EN.O.A2.1.6 Euler turbomachine equation. For steady flow through a rotor, specific work done on the fluid is w = u₂c_θ2 − u₁c_θ1 (pump or compressor); for a turbine the extracted work is

its negative. - EN.O.A2.1.7 Water hammer (Joukowsky surge Δp = ρ a ΔV for instantaneous valve closure in an elastic pipe). - **EN.O.A2.2 External flows.** Drag and lift coefficients; boundary layer; separation as the stall and form-drag mechanism. Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = UL/ν (the two forms are equivalent, uses PH.O.A1.5). Flight mechanics and aeroelasticity draw on this cell plus EN.O.A1. - **EN.O.A2.3 Free-surface flows.** - EN.O.A2.3.1 Open-channel specific energy and Froude number Fr = V/√(g h) for a rectangular channel. - EN.O.A2.3.2 Manning equation, an empirical resistance closure

for steady, uniform, fully rough open-channel flow. - EN.O.A2.3.3 Ship hydrostatics and stability: buoyancy, metacentric height GM, righting arm, for small heel angles (initial stability). - EN.O.A2.3.4 Hull resistance and seakeeping, with Froude scaling of wave resistance. - **EN.O.A2.4 Compressible and acoustic flows.** - EN.O.A2.4.1 Isentropic nozzle relations for a calorically perfect gas in adiabatic, reversible, quasi-one-dimensional flow. Choked flow when the throat is sonic (M = 1). - EN.O.A2.4.2 Normal-shock relations (Rankine–Hugoniot) for a perfect gas. - EN.O.A2.4.3 Linear acoustics: small-amplitude pressure waves in a quiescent fluid; sound pressure

level and transmission loss (noise control). - **EN.O.A2.5 Porous-medium flows.** - EN.O.A2.5.1 Darcy's law q = −(k/μ)∇p for slow, laminar flow through a rigid, saturated porous medium. CONTESTED: EA.O.A4 (groundwater) is the alternative owner. - EN.O.A2.5.2 Ergun equation for pressure drop through a packed bed of particles. - EN.O.A2.5.3 Consolidation (Terzaghi one-dimensional consolidation) for saturated, linear, laterally confined soil. Concepts for A2: control volume versus particle, streamline, stagnation, cavitation (local pressure falls to vapour pressure), multiphase regime maps. ### EN.O.A3 Energy and entropy Situation. Every efficiency claim and thermal sizing

is the first law on a control volume, bounded by the second law and closed by a rate law. Complication. v1 lacked a key line and misstated the Stefan–Boltzmann exchange (audit fact check). Question. Which mechanisms exhaust energy-and-entropy models in engineering? Key line. Plural noun: energy mechanisms. Dimension: what the model asks of the energy. Order: from bookkeeping to limit to rate to source. Members (4): first-law balances; second-law limits; heat-transfer rates; reacting energy. - **EN.O.A3.1 First-law balances.** - EN.O.A3.1.1 Steady open-system first law: Q̇ − Ẇ = Σṁ(h +

V²/2 + g z)out − Σṁ(h + V²/2 + g z)in, with heat in and work out positive. The law is owned by physics (uses PH.O.A4.1). - EN.O.A3.1.2 Property closures: ideal-gas model, steam and refrigerant tables (data, W12 and W4). - EN.O.A3.1.3 Cycles as applications: Rankine, Brayton, Otto, Diesel (air-standard idealisations), vapour-compression refrigeration with COP = Q_cold / W. - **EN.O.A3.2 Second-law limits.** - EN.O.A3.2.1 Carnot efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h, the ceiling for a heat engine between two reservoirs at absolute temperatures. Uses PH.O.A4.1. - EN.O.A3.2.2 Exergy: work potential relative

to a stated dead state. Irreversibility located per component, not only totalled. - EN.O.A3.2.3 Pinch analysis: minimum approach temperature in a heat-exchanger network. - **EN.O.A3.3 Heat-transfer rates.** - EN.O.A3.3.1 Fourier's law q = −k∇T for an isotropic conductor; plane wall Q = k A ΔT / L at steady state. CONTESTED: PH.O.A4.1 (transport) is the alternative owner. - EN.O.A3.3.2 Newton's law of cooling q = h A (T_s − T_∞), with h from a Nusselt correlation used inside its stated Re and Pr range. - EN.O.A3.3.3 Radiation exchange. Emissive power

of a grey surface is ε σ T⁴. Net exchange of a small grey surface with large surroundings is q = ε σ A (T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴), absolute temperatures (Incropera and DeWitt, ch. 1). Enclosures use view factors. - EN.O.A3.3.4 Heat exchangers: LMTD method, or effectiveness–NTU with NTU = U A / C_min. - EN.O.A3.3.5 Fins: added area against a convection boundary, with fin efficiency. - **EN.O.A3.4 Reacting energy.** Heating value and stoichiometry enter the first law as an enthalpy of reaction (uses CH.O.A3.1). Adiabatic flame temperature is the no-heat-loss

limit. Fire growth and smoke models for compartments draw on this cell (fire protection). ### EN.O.A4 Electromagnetic state Situation. Power and signal artefacts are closed by circuit or field laws. Complication. v1 held electromagnetic and information state in one cell, which made six closing quantities (audit EN #4). Information state now belongs to CS. Question. Which reductions of electromagnetic theory exhaust EN models of power and signal? Key line. Plural noun: electromagnetic reductions. Dimension: which reduction of Maxwell's equations closes the model. Order: from smallest to largest spatial extent relative

to wavelength, then down to the device. Members (4): lumped circuits; electromechanical conversion; distributed fields; semiconductor devices. Shared basis. Maxwell's equations, Faraday's law of induction and the Kirchhoff circuit laws (as the quasistatic reduction) are owned by physics (uses PH.O.A1.2b). EN owns the engineering reductions and device closures. - **EN.O.A4.1 Lumped circuits.** Valid when the circuit is small compared with the shortest relevant wavelength. - EN.O.A4.1.1 Ohm's law V = I R for a linear resistor; Kirchhoff circuit laws (uses PH.O.A1.2b). - EN.O.A4.1.2 Impedance R, jωL and 1/(jωC), with phasors,

for linear circuits in sinusoidal steady state. - EN.O.A4.1.3 Thévenin and Norton equivalents, for linear networks seen from two terminals. - EN.O.A4.1.4 Maximum power transfer. For a linear source with impedance Z_s, load power is maximised when Z_L = Z_s* (complex conjugate). A resistive match applies only to DC or purely resistive sources. A theorem, not a universal design rule. - EN.O.A4.1.5 Linear time-invariant system response: impulse response, transfer function, frequency response. Fourier and Laplace transforms are MA (uses MA.O.A4). State space ẋ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx

+ Du and G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D, for LTI plants. - EN.O.A4.1.6 Sampling theorem. A band-limited signal with no content at or above B is recovered from samples taken faster than 2B per second. Uses MA.B.C4 (MSC 94A). - EN.O.A4.1.7 Concepts: ground and reference, power factor, harmonics, noise figure. - **EN.O.A4.2 Electromechanical conversion.** - EN.O.A4.2.1 Magnetic circuit: Ampère's law with reluctance, for linear core material without saturation. - EN.O.A4.2.2 Ideal transformer V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, for zero leakage, zero winding resistance and infinite core permeability. - EN.O.A4.2.3 Machines:

torque from current and flux. Synchronous speed n_s = 120 f / p (rpm, p poles). Induction-motor slip. - EN.O.A4.2.4 Power-flow equations for an AC network in balanced steady state (load flow). - **EN.O.A4.3 Distributed fields.** - EN.O.A4.3.1 Transmission line: telegrapher's equations; characteristic impedance; reflection coefficient. - EN.O.A4.3.2 Waveguides and antennas: modes, gain, radiation pattern. - EN.O.A4.3.3 Friis transmission equation for far-field free-space links between matched, polarisation-aligned antennas. - EN.O.A4.3.4 Optical and photonic devices: fibre modes, attenuation, dispersion. Optics as physics (uses PH.O.A1.2c). - EN.O.A4.3.5 Electromagnetic compatibility: coupling paths and

shielding; skin effect. - **EN.O.A4.4 Semiconductor devices.** - EN.O.A4.4.1 Diode and MOSFET constitutive curves (e.g., Shockley diode equation for an ideal p–n junction with low injection). - EN.O.A4.4.2 Drift–diffusion device model (uses PH.O.A4.4a for band theory). - EN.O.A4.4.3 Digital abstraction: voltage bands treated as logic levels, with noise margins. Information-theoretic bounds (Shannon–Hartley) are not EN claims. For a band-limited channel with additive

Owner MA.B.C4 (MSC 94A); EN uses it in link budgets. ### EN.O.A5 Composition and microstructure Situation. Process and materials models are closed by conservation of species plus a rate or equilibrium law, and by the microstructure that supplies material properties. Complication. v1 had no key line here, and refiled Arrhenius, Raoult and Faraday electrolysis, which chemistry owns. Question. Which closures exhaust composition-and-microstructure models? Key line. Plural noun: composition

closures. Dimension: what closes the species or structure balance. Order: from reaction to separation to solid to charge to nucleus. Members (5): reaction rates; equilibrium stages; microstructure–property relations; electrochemical cells; neutron balances. - **EN.O.A5.1 Reaction rates.** - EN.O.A5.1.1 Species balance: accumulation = in − out + generation. - EN.O.A5.1.2 Ideal reactors: batch, continuous stirred tank (perfect mixing), plug flow (no axial mixing). range. Rate-based models apply when stage equilibrium fails. - EN.O.A5.2.4 Flowsheet degrees of freedom, recycle and purge. - **EN.O.A5.3 Microstructure–property relations.** - EN.O.A5.3.1 Phase diagram as the equilibrium map (uses CH.O.A3.1 for phase equilibrium). - EN.O.A5.3.2

TTT and CCT diagrams as kinetic maps for steels. - EN.O.A5.3.3 Hall–Petch relation σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2), for polycrystals over a stated grain-size range (fails at the nanoscale). - EN.O.A5.3.4 Rule of mixtures for composites, as upper (Voigt) and lower (Reuss) bounds, not a point prediction. - EN.O.A5.3.5 Dislocation slip as the mechanism of plastic flow (uses PH.O.A4.4 condensed matter). - **EN.O.A5.4 Electrochemical cells.** - EN.O.A5.4.1 Faraday's laws of electrolysis: mass reacted proportional to charge passed (uses CH.O.A3.1). Applied to corrosion rate and plating. - EN.O.A5.4.2 Nernst equation

for the reversible cell potential at stated activities (uses CH.O.A3.1). - EN.O.A5.4.3 Battery and fuel-cell device models: capacity, polarisation curves, state of charge. - EN.O.A5.4.4 Passivation as a kinetic state, not a permanent property. - **EN.O.A5.5 Neutron balances.** - EN.O.A5.5.1 Effective multiplication factor k_eff; criticality at k_eff = 1. - EN.O.A5.5.2 One-group neutron diffusion equation, valid away from boundaries and strong absorbers; transport theory otherwise. Cross-section data uses PH. - EN.O.A5.5.3 Decay heat after shutdown, carried as a source by the energy balance EN.O.A3.1. - EN.O.A5.5.4 Shielding attenuation for a

## 2. Governing thought Computer science is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five properties of a computation: correctness, cost, coordination, learning, and protection. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the property asserted of a computation.** Order: structural, from the single program outward to many agents and adversaries. 1. Correctness 2. Cost 3. Coordination 4. Learning 5. Protection ## 4. Face O — Objects ### CS.O.A1 Correctness **SCQA.** Situation. A computation is first judged by whether it does what it is

specified to do. Complication. Specifications, semantics and proof tools exist, but most software is never proved, and the specification itself may be wrong. Question. What can be claimed about correctness, by what means, and where do such claims stop? Answer. CS owns the meaning of programs, the specification and its verification, type discipline, testing, and the limits on all four. The undecidability theorems behind those limits are owned by MA (uses MA.O.A1). Key line (inductive; plural noun: correctness claims; dimension: the means by which agreement with intent is asserted; order:

from meaning, through proof and types, to sampling, then to limits). Members (5): Semantics · Specification and verification · Types · Testing · Limits of correctness. - CS.O.A1.1 Semantics of languages. **A program has a meaning that can be stated independently of any one implementation.** Operational, denotational and axiomatic semantics are three styles of stating it. Lambda calculus and Turing machines are equivalent in power (the theorem is MA.O.A1). - CS.O.A1.1.1 Operational semantics. A program's meaning can be given as a transition relation on configurations. Two implementations agree when they

realise the same relation on observable steps. - CS.O.A1.1.2 Denotational semantics. A program's meaning can be given as a mathematical object, such as a continuous function on a domain. Recursion is then a least fixed point (the fixed-point theorem is MA.O.A2). - CS.O.A1.1.3 Adequacy. Operational and denotational accounts of one language agree on observable outcomes only when an adequacy result is proved for that language. Adequacy is a per-language claim, not a general one. - CS.O.A1.1.4 Church–Turing thesis. Every effectively calculable function is Turing-computable. It is a thesis about the

informal notion, not a theorem. Its standing is CONTESTED between CS and PL (uses PL.O.A5). - CS.O.A1.2 Specification and verification. **A program can be proved to meet a formal specification, given a sound logic and a correct specification.** Hoare logic proves partial correctness; total correctness also needs termination. Model checking decides temporal properties of finite-state models. - CS.O.A1.2.1 Hoare triples. A triple {P} C {Q} states that if P holds before C and C terminates, Q holds after. Loops need an invariant supplied by a person or a tool. -

CS.O.A1.2.2 Termination. Total correctness needs a variant: a quantity in a well-founded order that each loop iteration decreases. No algorithm finds a variant for every terminating program (uses MA.O.A1). - CS.O.A1.2.3 Model checking. Temporal-logic properties of a finite-state model are decidable. Practical limits come from state-space explosion, which grows exponentially with the number of concurrent components. - CS.O.A1.2.4 Separation logic. Programs that share heap memory can be reasoned about locally when assertions describe disjoint heap regions. The frame rule carries a proof past code that touches other regions. - CS.O.A1.3

Types. **Well-typed programs do not go wrong, for languages whose type system is proved sound.** Soundness is shown as progress and preservation. - CS.O.A1.3.1 Progress and preservation. A well-typed term is either a value or can take a step, and stepping keeps its type. Together these rule out stuck states under the stated semantics. - CS.O.A1.3.2 Type inference. For the Hindley–Milner fragment, every typable term has a principal type that an algorithm finds. Extensions such as higher-rank polymorphism lose decidable full inference. - CS.O.A1.3.3 Curry–Howard correspondence. Types correspond to propositions

and terms to proofs, for stated pairs of type systems and logics. The correspondence itself is owned by MA (uses MA.O.A1); its use in proof assistants is CS. - CS.O.A1.4 Testing. **Testing can show the presence of bugs, never their absence (Dijkstra), for any input space too large to exhaust.** It samples behaviour; it does not prove. - CS.O.A1.4.1 Coverage criteria. Statement, branch and path coverage measure how much of a program a test suite exercises. High coverage does not imply a low residual defect rate. The size of the

gap is an empirical claim (W4). - CS.O.A1.4.2 Property-based testing. Random inputs drawn against a stated property find counterexamples a fixed suite misses. A pass is evidence of absence only within the input distribution used. - CS.O.A1.4.3 Mutation testing. A suite's strength can be estimated by the fraction of seeded faults it detects. The estimate assumes that seeded faults resemble real ones; that assumption is (UNVERIFIED) in general. - CS.O.A1.5 Limits of correctness. **No general procedure decides any non-trivial semantic property of programs.** Rice's theorem holds for Turing-complete languages. Uses

MA.O.A1. - CS.O.A1.5.1 Halting problem. No program decides, for every program and input, whether that program halts. The theorem is MA.O.A1; CS uses it as the root of verification limits. - CS.O.A1.5.2 Sound but incomplete analysis. Static analysers escape Rice's theorem by over-approximating: they may report false alarms but miss no error in the analysed class. Abstract interpretation is the general method. - CS.O.A1.5.3 Specification gap. A proof shows agreement with the specification, not with intent. Defects in the specification are outside what verification can catch. Named objects: operational semantics,

denotational semantics, lambda calculus, Church–Turing thesis, Hoare logic (hypotheses: sound rules, stated pre- and postconditions, partial correctness unless a variant is given), separation logic, model checking (hypothesis: a finite-state model), type soundness, Hindley–Milner inference, Curry–Howard correspondence, coverage, property-based testing, mutation testing (hypothesis: seeded faults represent real ones), Rice's theorem, halting problem, abstract interpretation (hypotheses: a lattice of abstract values and sound transfer functions). ### CS.O.A2 Cost **SCQA.** Situation. A correct computation may still be too slow, too large or too costly in energy. Complication. Costs are stated on abstract models,

but they are paid on real hardware with caches, pipelines and physical limits. Question. Which costs can be bounded, on which model, and how far do the bounds carry to machines? Answer. CS owns algorithms and data structures with their stated costs, the use of complexity classes, machine organisation, and the engineering limits of hardware. Complexity theorems are MA (uses MA.B.C3); device physics is PH. Key line (inductive; plural noun: cost claims; dimension: what bears the cost; order: from the procedure, to its data, to the problem class, to the

machine, to physics). Members (5): Algorithms · Data structures · Complexity classes · Machines and architecture · Physical limits of hardware. - CS.O.A2.1 Algorithms. **Each algorithm has a stated cost on a stated model.** Comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case (a decision-tree lower bound, uses MA.B.C3). - CS.O.A2.1.1 Asymptotic cost. Big-O statements bound growth up to a constant factor and beyond some input size. They do not rank two algorithms at a given practical size. - CS.O.A2.1.2 Design paradigms. Divide and conquer, dynamic programming and

greedy choice each apply when a stated structural property holds. Greedy choice is optimal only under a matroid-like exchange property. - CS.O.A2.1.3 Randomised algorithms. An algorithm with access to random bits may have lower expected cost or simpler structure. Its guarantee is a probability over its own coins, not over inputs (uses MA.O.A5). - CS.O.A2.1.4 Approximation. For some NP-hard optimisation problems, polynomial algorithms reach a stated ratio of the optimum. For others, no such ratio is reachable unless P = NP (uses MA.B.C3). - CS.O.A2.2 Data structures. **A data structure

trades the cost of one operation against another, and amortised analysis bounds the total over a sequence.** Union–find with path compression and union by rank runs in O(α(n)) amortised time per operation. - CS.O.A2.2.1 Amortised analysis. A sequence of m operations can cost less than m times the worst single operation. The potential method makes the bound exact for a stated sequence model. - CS.O.A2.2.2 Hashing. Hash tables give expected constant-time lookup under a uniform-hashing or universal-family assumption. Adversarial keys defeat a fixed hash function. - CS.O.A2.2.3 Balanced search trees.

Red–black and AVL trees keep height O(log n), so search, insert and delete run in O(log n) worst-case time. - CS.O.A2.2.4 External memory. When data exceed fast memory, cost is better counted in block transfers than in operations. B-trees are designed for that model. - CS.O.A2.3 Complexity classes. **Problems fall into classes by the resources a solving machine needs.** P, NP and PSPACE are the standard examples. Whether P = NP is OPEN and owned by MA.B.C3; CS uses it. - CS.O.A2.3.1 Reductions in practice. Showing a new problem NP-hard

by reduction is evidence that no efficient exact algorithm is likely. CS uses this to redirect effort to heuristics or approximation. - CS.O.A2.3.2 Hardness assumptions as engineering inputs. Cryptography and fine-grained complexity rest on stated conjectures, such as the exponential-time hypothesis. Results built on them are conditional (uses MA.B.C3). - CS.O.A2.3.3 Parameterised complexity. Some NP-hard problems are fast when a stated parameter is small. Fixed-parameter tractability is a claim about that parameter, not about the problem in general. - CS.O.A2.4 Machines and architecture. **Real cost depends on the memory hierarchy,

pipelines and parallelism of the machine.** Amdahl's law bounds speed-up by 1/((1−p) + p/s) for a fixed workload whose fraction p is parallelisable by a factor s. - CS.O.A2.4.1 Locality. Programs that reuse nearby data run faster on cached machines. The gap between cache and main-memory latency is large enough to reverse asymptotic rankings at practical sizes. - CS.O.A2.4.2 Gustafson's law. When the problem grows with the processor count, scaled speed-up is (1−p) + p·N. It does not contradict Amdahl's law; it changes the fixed quantity. - CS.O.A2.4.3 Instruction-level parallelism.

Pipelines and out-of-order execution overlap instructions. Data dependencies and branch mispredictions bound the achievable overlap. - CS.O.A2.4.4 Accelerators. Specialised hardware such as GPUs gives large speed-ups for regular, data-parallel work. Irregular control flow loses most of that gain. - CS.O.A2.5 Physical limits of hardware. **Hardware cost is bounded by engineering trends that are not laws.** Moore's law is an empirical trend, now slowing. Transistor physics is PH. - CS.O.A2.5.1 End of Dennard scaling. Power density no longer stays constant as transistors shrink. Clock rates have therefore plateaued, and designers turned

to many cores. Device causes are PH (uses PH.O.A4). - CS.O.A2.5.2 Landauer's bound. Erasing one bit dissipates at least kT ln 2 of energy. The principle is owned by PH (uses PH.O.A4); CS cites it as a floor far below current practice. - CS.O.A2.5.3 Energy as a cost measure. Energy per operation is now a first-class cost alongside time and space. Its measured values depend on the device and are W4 claims.
