nitrogen through fixation, which falls when soil mineral nitrogen is high. - **AG.O.A2.2 Water and irrigation.** Crop water use is estimated from weather and crop stage. Yield loss from a shortfall depends on crop and stage. - AG.O.A2.2.1 Crop water requirement. Crop evapotranspiration is a weather-based reference value times a crop coefficient (FAO-56). Hypotheses: the weather data represent the field, and the coefficient fits the crop, stage and climate (uses EA.O.A4.2). - AG.O.A2.2.2 Yield response to water. Relative yield loss is taken as proportional to relative evapotranspiration deficit through a

response factor. Hypotheses: the factor fits the crop and growth stage, and water is the only limit. - AG.O.A2.2.3 Irrigation scheduling. Water is applied when root-zone depletion reaches a chosen share of available water. Hypotheses: known root depth and soil water limits. Deficit irrigation raises water productivity only if stress falls in stages tolerant of it, which is tested by trial. - AG.O.A2.2.4 Salinity and sodicity. Sodium adsorption ratio compares sodium with calcium and magnesium in milliequivalents per litre. High values harm soil structure. Yield falls linearly above a crop-specific

salinity threshold in the Maas–Hoffman form (uses EA.O.A4.5). - **AG.O.A2.3 Crop management.** A practice changes yield, and the claim holds only for the stated season, site and population. Rotation, tillage, sowing. A yield claim must state season, site and population. - AG.O.A2.3.1 Rotation. The rotation effect is yield after a given preceding crop compared with continuous cropping in the same long-term trial. Its sign depends on crop sequence, disease carry-over and nitrogen left by legumes. - AG.O.A2.3.2 Tillage. Pooled comparisons report a lower average yield under no-till than under conventional

tillage. The gap narrows where residues are kept and crops are rotated. The size of the average gap is UNVERIFIED and depends on soil and climate. - AG.O.A2.3.3 Intercropping. The land equivalent ratio sums each crop's mixture yield divided by its sole-crop yield. A value above one means the mixture uses land better. Hypotheses: sole crops at their own best density and management, same site and season. - AG.O.A2.3.4 Phenology and sowing date. Crop development is modelled by thermal time accumulated above a base temperature. Hypotheses: development is linear between

base and upper thresholds, and the thresholds are known for the cultivar (uses EA.O.A4.3). - **AG.O.A2.4 Animal husbandry.** Animal performance is set by feed intake and its use, within a husbandry system and a welfare standard. Pastoral and housed systems, nutrition, welfare. NZ pastoral dairying is a substrate. - AG.O.A2.4.1 Energy requirement. Requirement for metabolisable energy is summed over maintenance, growth, pregnancy and lactation. Hypotheses: feed energy is measured on representative samples, and the requirement equations fit the animal class. Feed value by laboratory proxy needs calibration against animal trials.

- AG.O.A2.4.2 Stocking rate. Over a moderate range and at a given pasture supply, output per animal falls and output per hectare rises as stocking rate rises. The range and the turning point are tested by farmlet trials. - AG.O.A2.4.3 Rumen digestion and methane. Rumen microbes ferment fibre and release methane. Enteric methane per animal rises with feed intake. Emission per unit of product falls as productivity per animal rises, which is UNVERIFIED across systems. The impact is EV. - AG.O.A2.4.4 Welfare measurement. Welfare is assessed by animal-based measures such

as body condition score, lameness score and behaviour. Hypotheses: the scale suits the species and breed, and assessors are trained. A framework such as the Five Freedoms is a convention (W12), and welfare law is LA (uses LA.O.A1.1). - **AG.O.A2.5 Aquaculture, fisheries and forestry production.** Harvest is sustainable only if removal does not exceed production. Stock and stand models state the assumptions that make this checkable. - AG.O.A2.5.1 Surplus production. Maximum sustainable yield follows from logistic growth. Hypotheses: logistic growth, equilibrium, catch per unit effort proportional to abundance (uses BI.O.A5.1).

Maximum sustainable yield as a management target is CONTESTED. - AG.O.A2.5.2 Catch per unit effort. Catch per unit effort is an abundance index only if catchability is constant and effort is standardised. When fish aggregate, the index stays high as the stock falls, which is called hyperstability. - AG.O.A2.5.3 Forest stand growth. Stand volume follows a sigmoid curve. The age that maximises mean annual increment is where mean annual increment equals current annual increment. Hypotheses: a single stand, a growth curve for the site, and volume as the only objective.

- AG.O.A2.5.4 Feed conversion in aquaculture. Feed conversion ratio is feed given divided by live weight gained. It varies with species, temperature, size and feeding rate. Hypothesis: weights are taken over the same period and mortality is accounted for. Named objects: Liebig's law of the minimum (one limiting factor, no interaction); Mitscherlich response (other factors not limiting); soil test calibration; DRIS (reference population of the same crop); FAO-56 crop coefficient method (weather represents field); yield response factor (water the only limit); sodium adsorption ratio; Maas–Hoffman salinity response; land equivalent ratio;

thermal time model; stocking rate; body condition scoring; Beverton–Holt yield-per-recruit (constant recruitment, known growth and natural mortality, steady state); virtual population analysis (known natural mortality, accurate catch at age, closed stock); surplus production model; mean annual increment; feed conversion ratio. ### AG.O.A3 Crop and animal health **SCQA.** Situation. Producing organisms fall ill and are attacked by pests, weeds and pathogens. Loss is limited by detection, diagnosis and control. Complication. Veterinary medicine borders human medicine, and BI.O.A3.5 also lists animal disorder. Control agents select for resistance, and border measures partly belong

to law. Question. How is the health of crops and animals kept, and what evidence shows that control works? Answer. AG owns the detection, diagnosis and control of harm to production organisms, with the spread models behind them. The pathogen's biology is BI, and human disease is MD. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: health measures; dimension: what is protected and where the measure acts; order: the crop, the animal, the border, then the animal–human interface). Members (4): Plant protection · Veterinary medicine · Biosecurity · Zoonoses. Key line: plant protection,

veterinary medicine, biosecurity, zoonoses. - **AG.O.A3.1 Plant protection.** Control is justified when pest density passes the level at which control pays. Resistance to a control is a selection response. Pests, weeds, pathogens; integrated pest management. - AG.O.A3.1.1 Economic injury level. The injury level is control cost divided by crop value times damage per pest times control efficacy. The economic threshold is set below it to leave time to act. Hypotheses: damage is linear in density, and cost, value and efficacy are known and constant. - AG.O.A3.1.2 Resistance management. Resistance to

a pesticide or a resistant cultivar evolves under selection (uses BI.O.A4.1). The high-dose and refuge strategy delays it. Hypotheses: resistance is recessive and rare, and survivors mate at random with refuge insects. - AG.O.A3.1.3 Biological control. Classical biological control introduces a natural enemy from the pest's region of origin. Success is shown by lower pest density against a comparison site. Host specificity is tested before release (uses BI.O.A5.2). - AG.O.A3.1.4 Critical period of weed control. The critical period is the stage window in which weeds must be removed to keep

yield loss within a set limit. Its length depends on crop, weed density and relative time of emergence. - **AG.O.A3.2 Veterinary medicine.** A veterinary claim states the species, the test or intervention, and its measured accuracy or effect. Diagnosis and treatment of animal disorders. CONTESTED: BI.O.A3.5 also claims animal disorder, diagnosis and treatment; the alternative for all disorders is MD. - AG.O.A3.2.1 Test accuracy in animals. Sensitivity and specificity are measured against a reference standard, and predictive values change with prevalence (uses MD.O.A3.2). The Rogan–Gladen estimator corrects apparent prevalence. Hypothesis:

sensitivity and specificity are known and constant across populations. - AG.O.A3.2.2 Withholding periods. A withholding period is set so that residues in milk or meat fall below a limit after the last dose. It comes from depletion studies on the species and product. The safety limit is MD (uses MD.O.A4.4.1). - AG.O.A3.2.3 Antimicrobial use and resistance. Antimicrobial use in an animal group raises the frequency of resistance in its bacteria (uses MD.O.A2.1.1). The share of human resistance traced to animal use differs by organism and is CONTESTED. - AG.O.A3.2.4 Trials

in veterinary practice. The herd, not the animal, is the unit of randomisation when infection spreads between animals. Hypotheses of the randomised trial: random assignment, no spillover between units, adequate sample size. - **AG.O.A3.3 Biosecurity.** Biosecurity lowers the chance and cost of an organism entering, establishing or spreading. Its measures are judged by detection and eradication outcomes. Border and incursion management (e.g. Mycoplasma bovis in NZ from 2017, UNVERIFIED date). - AG.O.A3.3.1 Inspection and sampling. A clean sample of n units from a large lot gives only an upper bound

of about 3/n on the infested fraction, at 95 per cent confidence (uses MA.O.A5). Hypotheses: random, independent sampling and a perfect test. - AG.O.A3.3.2 Surveillance sensitivity. For n units sampled at random, the chance of detecting disease at design prevalence p is 1 − (1 − Se·p)^n, with test sensitivity Se (uses MA.O.A5). A claim of freedom depends on the assumed design prevalence. - AG.O.A3.3.3 Eradication feasibility. Eradication needs the effective reproduction number held below one (uses MD.O.A5.2). Spread between farms follows movement networks, and heterogeneous contact can invalidate a

homogeneous-mixing threshold (uses MD.O.A5.2.3). - AG.O.A3.3.4 Establishment of introduced pests. The chance of establishment rises with propagule pressure, the number of individuals and of release events. The harm to native ecosystems is EV (uses EV.O.A1.4). The harm to production is here. - **AG.O.A3.4 Zoonoses.** A zoonosis is an infection shared by animals and people, and AG owns the animal-host side of its maintenance and control. The animal side is AG; human disease is MD (One Health is a bridge). - AG.O.A3.4.1 Reservoirs. A reservoir is a population that maintains the

pathogen without outside input. It is identified by infection data from the host and evidence that the host supplies transmission. Brushtail possums and bovine tuberculosis in NZ are a standard case. - AG.O.A3.4.2 Control at source. Vaccinating or culling animals lowers human cases only if the animal route dominates. This is tested by human incidence before and after control, against a comparison (uses MD.O.A5.1). - AG.O.A3.4.3 Spillover. Predicting which animal pathogens will spill over to people is an OPEN programme. Contact rate, prevalence and infection per contact are measured, but

host traits predict emergence poorly (UNVERIFIED strength). - AG.O.A3.4.4 Foodborne zoonoses. On-farm control and processing control contribute separately to human foodborne cases. Source attribution apportions cases using stated model assumptions (uses MD.O.A5.1). Named objects: economic injury level (damage linear in density, constants known); economic threshold; high-dose and refuge strategy (recessive rare resistance, random mating); classical biological control; critical period of weed control; Rogan–Gladen estimator (known sensitivity and specificity); withholding period; rule of three for zero-positive samples (random sampling); surveillance sensitivity formula; design prevalence; reservoir; propagule pressure; One Health. ### AG.O.A4

Food **SCQA.** Situation. Produce becomes food through composition, processing, safety control and specification. Complication. The molecule is CH, human nutritional need is MD, and the legal force of a standard is LA. v1 blended these in one cell. Question. What makes food safe, nutritious and stable, and how is that stated so it can be checked? Answer. AG owns the composition of food as a product, the kinetics of processing, the control of hazards, and the standards as stipulations. Chemistry, human need and law keep their own claims. **Key line**

(inductive; plural noun: food properties and controls; dimension: what is asserted about the food; order: what it is, how it is kept stable, how it is made safe, how it is specified). Members (4): Composition and nutrition · Processing and preservation · Food safety · Food standards. Key line: composition and nutrition, processing, safety, standards. - **AG.O.A4.1 Composition and nutrition.** The composition of a food is a measured amount of components by a stated method. It varies with variety, season and processing. The molecule is CH; human nutritional need is

MD. - AG.O.A4.1.1 Proximate analysis. Moisture, ash, protein, fat and carbohydrate by difference are reported by stated methods. Protein is Kjeldahl nitrogen times a conversion factor, commonly 6.25, which assumes a typical nitrogen share (uses CH.O.A5.3). Oven drying needs constant mass and negligible loss of other volatiles. - AG.O.A4.1.2 Natural variation. A composition table gives a mean with variation. One sample does not equal the table value. A label claim must state its basis, such as per 100 g as sold or as eaten. - AG.O.A4.1.3 Retention in processing. Nutrient

loss on cooking and storage is described by measured retention factors for a stated food, temperature and time. Hypothesis for a first-order model: loss rate is proportional to the amount present (uses CH.O.A4.1). - AG.O.A4.1.4 Food security measures. The Food Insecurity Experience Scale uses Rasch scaling, with one underlying dimension, equal item discrimination and independent responses. CONTESTED: alternative homes are EC and MD.O.A5. - **AG.O.A4.2 Processing and preservation.** Preservation keeps food safe and stable by lowering water activity, temperature or pH, or by killing or inhibiting microbes. Each effect is

quantified. Fermentation, pasteurisation, drying. - AG.O.A4.2.1 Thermal death time. The D value is the time at a temperature for one tenfold reduction. The z value is the temperature change that changes D tenfold. Hypotheses: first-order death, known values for the target in that food, heat reaching the coldest point (uses CH.O.A4.2). - AG.O.A4.2.2 Water activity. Growth is not possible below a limiting water activity that differs by organism. Drying and salting act by lowering it. The moisture sorption isotherm links water content to water activity and shows hysteresis. - AG.O.A4.2.3

Pasteurisation. Pasteurisation is a stated time and temperature that gives a set reduction of target pathogens without sterilising. Milk pasteurisation is verified with the alkaline phosphatase test. Hypothesis: target organism and D and z values are chosen correctly. - AG.O.A4.2.4 Fermentation yield and growth. Ethanol yield from glucose cannot exceed 0.511 g per g by stoichiometry (uses CH.O.A1.2). Real yields are lower. Monod kinetics assume one limiting substrate and balanced growth (uses BI.O.A2.3). - **AG.O.A4.3 Food safety.** A food is safe in a stated sense when hazards are controlled to

the level a standard allows. This is shown by verified controls, not by end-product testing alone. HACCP as a control system (W11); pathogen limits. - AG.O.A4.3.1 HACCP principles. HACCP has seven principles: hazard analysis, critical control points, critical limits, monitoring, corrective action, verification and record keeping. Hypotheses: hazards are identified correctly, prerequisite programmes operate, and critical limits are validated. - AG.O.A4.3.2 End-product testing. The chance of detecting a contaminated lot is one minus (1 − p)^n for n random samples at contamination proportion p (uses MA.O.A5). Hypothesis: random spread of

the contaminant. Clustering makes a sampling plan overstate assurance. - AG.O.A4.3.3 Predictive microbiology. Primary models give growth over time. Secondary models give growth rate against temperature, pH and water activity. Hypotheses: conditions lie within the fitted range, and the strain behaves like the fitted strains. Challenge tests check the model. - AG.O.A4.3.4 Chemical hazards. Mycotoxins in grain are concentrated in few kernels, so sampling error dominates the measured concentration. Residues, allergens and mycotoxins are controlled by limits and by sampling plans with stated uncertainty. - **AG.O.A4.4 Food standards.** A food

standard is a stipulated specification (W12). Its content is set by a standard-setting body, and its legal force is a legal claim. Codex Alimentarius; FSANZ for Australia and NZ (W12; legal force LA). - AG.O.A4.4.1 Codex Alimentarius. Codex texts are international standards, guidelines and codes of practice. They bind a state only when adopted. The WTO Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures refers to them (uses LA.O.A1.4). - AG.O.A4.4.2 Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. FSANZ develops the Code. The Code has legal effect through legislation in

each jurisdiction (uses LA.O.A1.1). The content of a limit is AG, and its enforcement is LA. - AG.O.A4.4.3 Maximum residue limits. A limit rests on supervised residue trials under good practice, then a check that estimated intake stays below a health-based reference value (uses MD). Compliance is tested by sampling and analysis with stated measurement uncertainty. - AG.O.A4.4.4 Labelling and certification. Organic certification verifies a production process against a written standard and does not guarantee a residue-free product. Origin and nutrient claims are definitions (W12) checked by inspection. Named objects:

proximate analysis; Kjeldahl method (nitrogen-to-protein factor assumed); food composition table; thermal death time D and z (first-order death, coldest point reached); water activity; pasteurisation; Monod growth model (one limiting substrate, balanced growth); HACCP (hazards correctly identified, validated limits); predictive microbiology (fitted range); Codex standard; FSANZ Code; maximum residue limit; organic certification. ### AG.O.A5 Farming systems **SCQA.** Situation. Farms are systems of land, organisms, labour and markets, and outcomes arise from the interaction of the parts. Complication. Farm economics and prices are EC, and environmental impact is EV. Productivity measurement and

farm decisions sit between them and had no single home. Question. How are a farm's output, decisions and environmental load measured and placed? Answer. AG owns the measurement of farm physical productivity, the decision methods applied to farms, and the practice-level load that farming creates. EC owns prices and welfare, and EV owns the impact. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: whole-farm questions; dimension: what is asked of the farm as a whole; order: what it produces, how it is run, what it releases). Members (3): System productivity · Farm management

· Environmental effect of farming. Key line: system productivity, farm management, environmental effect. - **AG.O.A5.1 System productivity.** Farm productivity is a ratio of aggregate output to aggregate input. Measured change depends on the index and the inputs counted. Total factor productivity of farms (measurement here; economics EC). - AG.O.A5.1.1 Partial and total productivity. Yield per hectare and output per worker rise when other inputs substitute, so partial measures do not show efficiency. A total factor index weights inputs by cost share. Cost shares stand for output elasticities only under competitive

input markets and constant returns (uses EC.O.A4.1). - AG.O.A5.1.2 Yield gap. The yield gap is potential yield from a validated crop model minus actual yield. Hypotheses: the model is validated for the site and cultivar, and the weather record represents the period. Part of the gap is not economically closable. - AG.O.A5.1.3 Livestock system efficiency. Output per unit of feed or per hectare ranks systems differently when the system boundary changes, such as with or without imported feed. A comparison must state the boundary and the feed accounted for. -

**AG.O.A5.2 Farm management.** A farm decision is evaluated by what changes in returns and costs, with risk stated. Decisions under weather and price risk. - AG.O.A5.2.1 Gross margin and partial budget. Gross margin is enterprise output minus variable costs. A partial budget counts only the costs and returns that change. Hypotheses: variable costs are allocable, fixed costs are unchanged, everything else stays the same (uses EC). - AG.O.A5.2.2 Investment appraisal. Net present value discounts forecast cash flows. Hypotheses: the cash flows are forecast with stated error, and the discount rate

reflects the risk. A positive value is a forecast, not a result. - AG.O.A5.2.3 Income risk. Diversification lowers income variance only if enterprise returns are not perfectly positively correlated (uses MA.O.A5). Insurance and forward contracts transfer risk and carry a cost. The claim is tested on farm records. - AG.O.A5.2.4 Whole-farm models. A whole-farm linear programme assumes linear constraints, known coefficients and one objective (uses MA). Its optimum is optimal for the model. It is a decision aid and is not evidence about the farm. - **AG.O.A5.3 Environmental effect of

farming.** AG owns the practice and the farm-level load it produces, and EV owns the effect on the receiving environment. Nitrate leaching, methane. The impact claim is EV; AG owns the practice that changes it. - AG.O.A5.3.1 Nitrogen balance. Farm-gate nitrogen surplus is inputs minus nitrogen in products. It indicates loss potential and does not give the loss path. Hypotheses: the boundary is defined and all significant flows are counted. Urine patches in grazed pasture concentrate the load (uses EV.O.A2.2). - AG.O.A5.3.2 Methane intensity and total. Emission per unit of

product can fall while total emission rises if output rises. Both figures must be stated. Inventories use emission factors per animal class (uses EV.O.A1.1). - AG.O.A5.3.3 Mitigation effect. A mitigation practice, such as a nitrification inhibitor or riparian planting, has an effect size that depends on site. A plot-scale result need not hold at farm or catchment scale. Transfer is tested by trial at the larger scale. - AG.O.A5.3.4 Soil carbon change. Practice changes soil organic carbon slowly compared with sampling error. Detection needs paired sampling on an equivalent soil

mass basis, many samples and several years (uses EA.O.A4.5). Named objects: total factor productivity (competitive input markets, constant returns for the cost-share reading); yield gap (validated crop model); gross margin; partial budgeting (other things unchanged); net present value (forecast flows, risk-based discount rate); whole-farm linear programme (linear, known coefficients); nitrogen balance (defined boundary); mass balance; equivalent soil mass sampling.

## 2. Governing thought Environmental science is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five links of a coupled system: pressures, states, impacts, responses, and limits. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the link in the human–environment causal chain.** Order: causal. 1. Pressures 2. States 3. Impacts 4. Responses 5. Limits ## 4. Face O — Objects Each A-cell gives a Situation, Complication, Question and Answer, then its key line, its sub-cells and the named objects it owns. Each sub-cell opens with

a bold claim. Child cells below a sub-cell state one testable claim each. Where a model or method is named, its hypotheses are stated in the same sentence (R5). ### EV.O.A1 Pressures **SCQA.** Situation. People load the environment by what they release, convert, remove and introduce. Complication. Loads are described by activity (farming, transport), by medium (air, water) and by receptor, and v1 mixed the three. A load was also confused with its effect. Question. Which loads, from which activities, in what units? Answer. A pressure claim names a flux

or a change imposed by people, in stated units over a stated period. It does not assert the effect, which is A3. Drivers, the activities that create a load, are grouped under pressures and are not a sixth key-line cell. Key line (inductive; plural noun: pressure types; dimension: what people do to the environment; order: structural, from material added to organisms added). Members (4): Emissions · Land and sea use change · Extraction · Introduced species. - EV.O.A1.1 Emissions — greenhouse gases, pollutants. **An emission is a flux of a

substance or energy from a source to the environment, stated per period and per unit of activity.** Inventories follow IPCC guidelines (W12 for method). - EV.O.A1.1.1 Greenhouse gas inventories. IPCC guidelines define tiers. Tier 1 multiplies activity data by a default emission factor. Higher tiers use country-specific factors or process models. Hypotheses: the activity data are complete, and the factor represents the local process. - EV.O.A1.1.2 Warming potential metrics. Global warming potential converts a gas to carbon dioxide equivalent over a stated horizon, commonly 100 years. The horizon changes the

weight of short-lived gases such as methane. Hypotheses: a pulse emission, a fixed horizon and carbon dioxide as reference. The convention is W12; the radiative physics is EA.O.A4.3. - EV.O.A1.1.3 Primary and secondary pollutants. Sulphur dioxide and particles leave a source directly. Ground-level ozone forms in the air from precursors, so its concentration is a state (EV.O.A2.1), not an emission. The formation chemistry is CH.O.A4.5. - EV.O.A1.1.4 Point and diffuse discharges. A point source is measured at the outfall. A diffuse source is estimated from land use, rainfall and soil.

A load is flow times concentration integrated over the period, so a concentration alone is not a load. - EV.O.A1.2 Land and sea use change — clearance, drainage, urbanisation. **A land or sea use change is a documented conversion of cover or management, measured as area by class between two dates.** - EV.O.A1.2.1 Cover conversion from imagery. Change is reported from classified imagery, with accuracy stated by a confusion matrix. Area of change counted from mapped pixels is biased by classification error. An unbiased area needs a sample-based reference estimate.

- EV.O.A1.2.2 Habitat loss and fragmentation. Loss of habitat area and the splitting of the remainder are separate pressures. Whether fragmentation affects richness beyond the loss of area is CONTESTED (uses BI.O.A5.5). - EV.O.A1.2.3 Hydrological modification. Drainage, damming and channelisation alter the flow regime: its magnitude, timing and frequency. Replacing permeable with impervious cover raises peak runoff for a given rainfall. Flow as a water-balance term is EA.O.A4.2. - EV.O.A1.2.4 Seabed and coastal disturbance. Bottom trawling, dredging, reclamation and farm structures alter the seabed. The pressure is the area and

frequency of disturbance. The effect on benthic communities is a later claim (EV.O.A3.1). - EV.O.A1.3 Extraction — water, fish, minerals. **An extraction is a removal of water, organisms or minerals from a stock, stated as a rate against the stock's size or renewal.** Fishing and the fishery are one taking, not two cells. - EV.O.A1.3.1 Water abstraction. A take is consumptive when the water is not returned to its source. Allocation is measured as volume per period against flow or recharge. A legal allocation is LA; the hydrology is EA.O.A4.2.

- EV.O.A1.3.2 Harvest of living stocks. Harvest pressure is catch relative to stock size or production. The Schaefer surplus production model gives maximum sustainable yield. Hypotheses: logistic growth, equilibrium, and catch per unit effort proportional to abundance. Maximum sustainable yield as a target is CONTESTED (uses BI.O.A5.1). The production system is AG.O.A2.5. - EV.O.A1.3.3 Mineral and aggregate extraction. Mining and quarrying remove a non-renewable stock and create waste rock and tailings. The pressure is the area disturbed and the mass moved. Deposit geology is EA.O.A1.5. - EV.O.A1.3.4 Forest and biomass

removal. Removal is volume per area per year against the growth increment. The Faustmann rotation gives the harvest age that maximises land value. Hypotheses: a known growth function, constant prices, costs and interest rate, and replanting after each harvest (uses EC). - EV.O.A1.4 Introduced species — pests and invasives (e.g. possums and mustelids in NZ). **An introduction is a documented arrival of a species outside its historical range through human agency, with the pathway recorded.** - EV.O.A1.4.1 Pathways and vectors. Deliberate pathways include horticulture and acclimatisation. Accidental ones include hull

fouling, ballast water and contaminated goods. Pathway risk is counted as arrivals per pathway per year. - EV.O.A1.4.2 Propagule pressure. Propagule pressure is the number of individuals and of release events. Higher propagule pressure raises the probability of establishment. Border measures that lower it are AG.O.A3.3. - EV.O.A1.4.3 Invasion stages. An invasion passes through transport, introduction, establishment and spread. The fraction passing each stage is estimated from records. The tens rule, about one in ten per stage, is a heuristic and its fit varies by taxon (UNVERIFIED). - EV.O.A1.4.4 Pest

density as pressure. A pest's damage depends on its density. Control aims at a density below a stated damage threshold. For possums and mustelids the pressure is predator density, and the effect on prey is EV.O.A3.1 (uses BI.O.A5.2). Named objects: emission factor and activity data (hypotheses above), global warming potential (pulse emission, fixed horizon, carbon dioxide as reference), load (flow times concentration), land-cover class and confusion matrix, flow regime, propagule pressure, surplus production model (logistic growth, equilibrium, catch per unit effort proportional to abundance), material flow analysis (system boundary and

period defined, every significant flow counted), Faustmann rotation (uses EC). ### EV.O.A2 States **SCQA.** Situation. Pressures, and natural processes, change the condition of air, water, soil and living systems. Complication. State claims were mixed with process explanations owned by EA, CH and BI, and with impacts. A concentration is a state; the harm it does is an impact. Question. What is the measured condition, and against what reference? Answer. A state claim reports a measured quantity at stated sites and dates with its uncertainty. When it judges, it names the

reference condition or standard. Key line (inductive; plural noun: states; dimension: what the state describes; order: structural, from continuous condition to episodic event to stock). Members (3): Measured conditions · Natural hazards and processes · Natural resources. - EV.O.A2.7 Measured conditions — air, freshwater, marine, soil, and biodiversity. **A measured condition is a quantity observed at stated places and times and reported with its uncertainty.** - EV.O.A2.1 Air quality — the measurement uses CH and EA. **Air quality is a measured concentration of a stated pollutant, averaged over a stated

time, against a stated guideline.** - EV.O.A2.1.1 Particulate matter. Particles are reported as mass concentration below 2.5 micrometres (PM2.5) or 10 micrometres (PM10) aerodynamic diameter. Continuous monitors need calibration against reference gravimetric measurement. The exposure–response is MD.O.A2.4. - EV.O.A2.1.2 Averaging time and exceedance. Guideline values are tied to averaging times. A site can meet an annual mean and exceed a 24-hour value. Exceedance counts depend on monitor siting and data completeness rules. - EV.O.A2.1.3 Dispersion and airsheds. Concentration at a site depends on emission and weather. The Gaussian plume model

gives downwind concentration. Hypotheses: steady emission rate, steady wind and uniform turbulence, flat terrain, and no reaction or deposition. A stable inversion keeps emissions near the ground (uses EA.O.A4.3). - EV.O.A2.1.4 Source apportionment. Receptor models estimate source shares of ambient particles from measured composition. Hypotheses: mass is conserved between source and receptor, source profiles are stable, and the mix is linear. Collinear sources cannot be separated. - EV.O.A2.2 Freshwater quality — nitrate, E. coli, sediment. **Freshwater quality is a set of measured concentrations and indicators in a stated water body,

compared with a numeric attribute or guideline.** - EV.O.A2.2.1 Nutrients and algal response. Nitrogen and phosphorus concentrations are states. Algal biomass, measured as chlorophyll a, is the response state. Liebig's law of the minimum holds when one resource limits growth at a time. Co-limitation is also documented, so the limiting nutrient is a claim for each site. - EV.O.A2.2.2 Faecal indicators. Escherichia coli is a faecal indicator. It shows faecal contamination, not the presence of a named pathogen. The link from concentration to illness risk is epidemiological (MD.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A2.2.3

Oxygen and organic load. Five-day biochemical oxygen demand measures degradable load. Hypotheses: incubation at 20 degrees Celsius in the dark, a suitable microbial seed, and no toxic inhibition. The Streeter–Phelps model gives the oxygen sag below a discharge. Hypotheses: steady flow, a single point source, and first-order decay and reaeration (uses CH.O.A4.1). - EV.O.A2.2.4 Sediment and clarity. Suspended sediment is mass per volume. Turbidity and visual clarity are optical proxies that need site-specific calibration to mass. Sediment source and transport are EA.O.A4.1. - EV.O.A2.3 Marine environment — acidification, warming. **The

marine state is a measured condition of seawater, seabed or coast at stated places and depths, reported against a stated baseline.** - EV.O.A2.3.1 Acidification. Seawater pH falls as the ocean takes up carbon dioxide. Carbonate chemistry links dissolved inorganic carbon, alkalinity and pH (uses CH.O.A3.4). The decline since the pre-industrial period is of the order of 0.1 pH units (UNVERIFIED figure). - EV.O.A2.3.2 Warming and marine heatwaves. Sea surface temperature is reported as an anomaly against a stated baseline period. A marine heatwave is defined by exceeding a percentile threshold

for a minimum duration (W12). Each study must state both. The ocean state is EA.O.A4.3. - EV.O.A2.3.3 Coastal habitat extent. Extent of seagrass, mangrove and kelp is reported as area with mapping accuracy. Loss of extent is a state. Its cause is a pressure claim (EV.O.A1.2) or an attribution claim (EV.O.A3.3). - EV.O.A2.3.4 Marine debris. Debris is reported as items or mass per area or volume. Microplastic is conventionally particles below 5 mm (W12). Counts depend on mesh size and method, so counts from different methods are not comparable. -

EV.O.A2.4 Soil state — contamination, erosion. **Soil state is a measured property of a soil profile at a stated depth and date, compared with a stated reference or limit.** The soil body is EA.O.A4.5. - EV.O.A2.4.1 Contaminant concentration and availability. A total concentration overstates risk where the contaminant is tightly bound. The bioavailable fraction depends on soil chemistry (uses CH). Guideline values apply to a stated land use. - EV.O.A2.4.2 Erosion rate. The Universal Soil Loss Equation multiplies rainfall, soil, slope, cover and practice factors. Hypotheses: sheet and rill erosion

only, a long-term average, and factors calibrated for the region. Gully erosion and landslides are outside it. The process is EA.O.A4.1. - EV.O.A2.4.3 Soil organic carbon stock. A stock is concentration times bulk density times depth. When bulk density changes, a change in stock is compared at equivalent soil mass, not at fixed depth. Detecting change needs repeat sampling by one protocol. - EV.O.A2.5 Biodiversity status — threat classifications (IUCN Red List criteria, W12). **Biodiversity status is a measured or assessed condition of a species, population or community, stated under

a named scheme.** - EV.O.A2.5.1 Threat categories. The IUCN Red List assigns a species to a category from Extinct to Least Concern by rules applied to estimates. Five criteria, A to E, assign the three threatened categories. Data Deficient and Not Evaluated sit outside the threat scale. National schemes differ, so a sentence names its scheme. - EV.O.A2.5.2 Abundance and detection. Counts are biased low where detection probability is below one. Occupancy models estimate detection from repeat visits. Hypotheses: the site is closed to change between visits, detections are independent,

and there are no false positives. - EV.O.A2.5.3 Richness and diversity indices. Richness is a count that depends on sampling effort. The Shannon index combines richness and evenness. Hypotheses: individuals are sampled at random, and every species present is represented. The species–area relation is a power law for areas of similar habitat and comparable effort (uses BI.O.A5.3). - EV.O.A2.5.4 Extinction declarations. A declaration of extinction needs surveys adequate to detect the species if it were present. Declarations are revisable because some species are rediscovered. A possibly-extinct tag records unresolved doubt.

Loss of a species as harm is EV.O.A3.1. - EV.O.A2.7.1 Reference condition. A condition is judged against a reference. The reference may be a pre-impact record, a least-disturbed site or a modelled expectation. The choice changes the classification of a site. A reference taken from a recently degraded state understates change. - EV.O.A2.7.2 Composite indices. An index combines several variables by stated weights and an aggregation rule. Two indices of one water body can rank sites differently. Hypotheses: weights and rule are stated before use. The index is W12 over

W4 inputs. - EV.O.A2.7.3 Trend detection. A trend claim needs a record long against its variability. The seasonal Kendall test detects a monotonic trend. Hypotheses: seasonal adjustment, and independent observations after adjustment. Serial correlation inflates significance (uses MA.O.A5). - EV.O.A2.6 Natural hazards and processes — geological, hydro-meteorological, and biogeochemical events. **A hazard event is stated by its magnitude, place and date, not by the harm it does.** An earthquake or a volcanic eruption is a state, not an impact. Flood, storm, drought, heat wave, and natural disaster are hydro-meteorological hazards.

- EV.O.A2.6.1 Geological events. An earthquake is reported by moment magnitude, a logarithmic scale of seismic moment, and by location. An eruption is reported by size and style. The process is EA.O.A2. CONTESTED: EA.O.A2.5 routes an eruption as a hazard event to EA.O.A5.5. - EV.O.A2.6.2 Hydro-meteorological events and return periods. An event is defined by exceeding a threshold. A return period T means an annual exceedance probability of 1/T. Extreme value analysis fits annual maxima. Hypotheses: independent maxima, a stationary record, and a record long against the return period sought.

Non-stationarity defeats it (uses EA.O.A4.2). - EV.O.A2.6.3 Wildfire. A wildfire is reported by area burned and intensity. A fire weather index states the condition of atmosphere and fuel. A human ignition is a pressure (EV.O.A1); the burned area is the state. - EV.O.A2.6.4 Biogeochemical episodes. Harmful algal blooms, hypoxic events and acid pulses are episodes of changed chemistry or biomass. Each is defined by a threshold in a measured variable. The mechanism is BI.O.A5.4 or EA.O.A4.2. The harm is EV.O.A3.1. - EV.O.A2.9 Natural resources — stocks of water, minerals, energy,

and living systems. **A natural resource is a stock stated by quantity, quality and renewal rate.** - EV.O.A2.9.1 Stock and renewal. A renewable stock is replaced at a rate. A non-renewable stock is not replaced on human time scales. A claim states both the stock and the rate. A drainage-basin water balance P = ET + Q + ΔS closes the account (uses EA.O.A4.2). - EV.O.A2.9.2 Resources and reserves. A mineral resource is a geological estimate. A reserve is the part recoverable under stated prices, technology and law. Reserve figures

change with price. The geology is EA.O.A1.5; the price is EC. - EV.O.A2.9.3 Status of harvested stocks. Status is biomass relative to a reference point. Reference points come from a stock model, so status depends on that model's hypotheses. The production model is under EV.O.A1.3 (uses BI.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A2.9.4 Natural capital accounts. Accounts record stocks and their changes in physical units. The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting is a statistical standard (W12). Monetary valuation of a stock is EC. The accounting method is EV.M.5. Environmental concepts are not a measured state.

A name for the field, a culture, or a teaching term is routed to its own field. Earth-system sciences are EA. Both placements are retired in the registry and the ids are not reused. Named objects: PM2.5 and PM10, Gaussian plume model (steady emission rate, steady wind and uniform turbulence, flat terrain, no reaction or deposition), receptor model (mass conserved, stable source profiles, linear mixing), Liebig's law of the minimum (one limiting resource at a time), five-day biochemical oxygen demand test (20 degrees Celsius, dark, seeded, no inhibition), Streeter–Phelps oxygen

sag model (steady flow, single point source, first-order decay and reaeration), Universal Soil Loss Equation (sheet and rill erosion, long-term average, regional calibration), IUCN Red List categories and criteria A to E, occupancy model (closure, independent detections, no false positives), Shannon index (random sample, all species represented), species–area relation (similar habitat, comparable effort), seasonal Kendall test (seasonal adjustment, independent observations), extreme value analysis and return period (independent maxima, stationary record, long record), reference condition. ### EV.O.A3 Impacts **SCQA.** Situation. A changed state harms ecosystems and people. Complication. Harm needs a

receptor, an exposure and a causal link. v1 held the physical model, the exposure–response and the valuation in one cell. Attribution is both a claim about shares of a pressure and a claim about a physical model. Question. What harm, to which receptor, attributed how? Answer. An impact claim names a receptor, a measured change in it, and the warrant that links the change to the pressure (W5 or W3). A correlation alone does not meet it. Risk is hazard times exposure times vulnerability (uses EA.O.A5.5); the hazard is EV.O.A2.6

and the rest is here. Key line (inductive; plural noun: impact claims; dimension: the object of the harm claim; order: structural, from ecosystem to person to link to benefit). Members (4): Ecosystem harm · Human health impact · Attribution · Ecosystem services. - EV.O.A3.1 Ecosystem harm — loss of function and species. **Ecosystem harm is a measured loss of function, composition or abundance at a stated site, attributed to a stated pressure.** - EV.O.A3.1.1 Toxic effect and species sensitivity. A species sensitivity distribution fits toxicity endpoints across species. The concentration

hazardous to 5 percent of species (HC5) is read from it. Hypotheses: tested species are a random sample of the community, endpoints are comparable, and the distribution shape fits the data. - EV.O.A3.1.2 Eutrophication effects. Enrichment raises algal biomass, which lowers dissolved oxygen as it decays. Each link in the chain is stated and measured. Recovery can lag after nutrient reduction because sediments release stored nutrients (uses BI.O.A5.4). - EV.O.A3.1.3 Extinction debt. Extinction debt is the delayed loss of species after habitat loss. The claim is that present richness exceeds

the equilibrium for the remaining area. Its size in real systems is OPEN (uses BI.O.A5.5). - EV.O.A3.1.4 Critical loads. A critical load is the highest deposition that causes no harmful long-term effect. Hypotheses: a steady-state mass balance, and a known chemical threshold for harm. Exceedance is deposition minus critical load (uses CH.O.A3.4). - EV.O.A3.2 Human health impact — the exposure–response is MD. **A health impact is a change in disease, injury or death in a population caused by an environmental exposure.** - EV.O.A3.2.1 Exposure assessment. Exposure is contact with an

agent through a pathway, not the ambient concentration. Personal exposure differs from a fixed-site measurement. Using an area average for individuals can bias the exposure–response estimate (uses MD.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A3.2.2 Reference doses. A reference dose is derived from tested doses with uncertainty factors, through a no-observed-adverse-effect level or a benchmark dose. Hypotheses: a threshold exists for the effect, the critical effect is identified, and the factors cover differences between species and between people (uses MD.O.A2.4). - EV.O.A3.2.3 Low-dose radiation. The linear no-threshold model takes risk as proportional to dose with

no safe threshold, for stochastic effects such as cancer. It is a protection assumption at low dose and is CONTESTED there. - EV.O.A3.2.4 Attributable fraction of illness. The population attributable fraction is p(RR − 1) / (1 + p(RR − 1)), with p the exposure prevalence and RR the relative risk. Hypotheses: the exposure causes the illness, the relative risk applies to this population, and confounding is controlled (uses MD.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A3.3 Attribution — the share of an observed change caused by a stated pressure (e.g. event attribution in climate

science). **An attribution claim states a share of change, its counterfactual and its uncertainty.** The physical model is EA. - EV.O.A3.3.1 Detection and attribution. Detection shows that a change exceeds internal variability. Attribution assigns the change to a cause against a counterfactual without that cause. A detected change is not thereby attributed (uses EA.O.A4.3). - EV.O.A3.3.2 Event attribution. Event attribution compares the probability of an event class with the pressure (P1) and without it (P0). The fraction of attributable risk is 1 − P0/P1. Hypotheses: models represent the event class,

and the event definition is fixed before analysis. Results depend on that definition (uses EA.O.A4.3). - EV.O.A3.3.3 Ecological attribution by design. A before–after–control–impact design attributes an ecological change to an activity. Hypotheses: control sites resemble the affected site, sampling occurs before and after at both, and controls are not affected (EV.M.2). - EV.O.A3.3.4 Interacting pressures. Where pressures interact, shares are not additive. Single-pressure attributions can sum to more or less than 100 percent. A claim states whether it assigns shares or marginal effects. - EV.O.A3.4 Ecosystem services — benefits people

receive; valuation is EC. **An ecosystem service is a benefit stated by its ecosystem function, its beneficiary and its unit.** - EV.O.A3.4.1 Service classification. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment groups services as provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting. Later schemes separate final from intermediate services. Adding supporting and final services double counts. The scheme is a convention (W12). - EV.O.A3.4.2 Biophysical supply. A service is first a measured flow, such as water purified, carbon stored or crop pollinated. A production function links ecosystem state to the flow. Supply is not value, and

a flow with no beneficiary is not a benefit. - EV.O.A3.4.3 Valuation methods. Valuation is owned by EC. Contingent valuation asks what people would pay for a described change. Hypotheses: respondents understand the change, hypothetical bias is controlled, and the sample represents those affected. Cost–benefit analysis needs effects valued in money and a stated discount rate (uses EC.O.A1.4, EC.O.A5.3). - EV.O.A3.4.4 Trade-offs between services. Services covary. Raising one, such as crop yield, often lowers another, such as water quality. A trade-off claim needs measured services at the same sites and

period (uses AG.O.A5.3). Named objects: species sensitivity distribution and HC5 (random sample of species, comparable endpoints, adequate distribution fit), critical load (steady-state mass balance, known chemical threshold), no-observed-adverse-effect level and benchmark dose (threshold exists, critical effect identified, uncertainty factors cover variation), linear no-threshold model (stochastic effects; CONTESTED at low dose), population attributable fraction (causal exposure, applicable relative risk, confounding controlled), fraction of attributable risk (event definition fixed, models represent the event class), detection and attribution, extinction debt (OPEN), contingent valuation and cost–benefit analysis (uses EC), ecosystem service. ### EV.O.A4 Responses

**SCQA.** Situation. Societies act to cut pressures, restore states or limit harm. Complication. A response claim mixes the intention, the instrument and the measured effect. Policy, price and duty belong to PO, EC and LA. Question. Which responses change a pressure or a state, and how is the change shown? Answer. EV owns the measured environmental effect of a response and the design that identifies it. The instrument is owned by PO, EC or LA. The effect is a W3 or W5 claim, not a statement of intent. Key line

(inductive; plural noun: responses; dimension: what the response acts on; order: structural, from ecosystem to place to emitter to works to practice). Members (5): Restoration · Conservation · Regulation · Environmental engineering · Kaitiakitanga. - EV.O.A4.1 Restoration — measured recovery after intervention. **A restoration claim states a measured recovery toward a reference after an intervention, with a control that separates it from natural recovery.** - EV.O.A4.1.1 Recovery trajectories. Recovery is measured against a reference state. Function, composition and structure recover at different rates, and a claim names which. A system

with alternative stable states may not return along its path of loss (EV.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A4.1.2 Active and passive restoration. Active restoration, such as planting, and passive restoration, by removing the pressure, are different interventions. A claim that active work is needed must be tested against a passive control. - EV.O.A4.1.3 Success criteria. Success is judged against targets set before the work. A monitoring period shorter than the recovery time can give a false failure or a false success. Reference sites must share the physical setting. - EV.O.A4.1.4 Bioremediation. Environmental biotechnology

uses organisms to remove or transform a contaminant. Rate is often modelled as first-order or Monod kinetics. Hypotheses: degraders are present, an electron acceptor is available, and the contaminant is bioavailable (uses BI.O.A2.3). - EV.O.A4.2 Conservation — protected areas, predator control (Predator Free 2050 is a stated goal, UNVERIFIED name and date). **A conservation claim states the effect of a protected area, species programme or pest control on a measured population or habitat, against a counterfactual.** - EV.O.A4.2.1 Protected area effect. The effect is the difference between protected land and

matched unprotected land. Protected areas are often sited where clearance was unlikely, so an unmatched comparison overstates the effect. - EV.O.A4.2.2 Systematic conservation planning. The method selects complementary sites that meet quantitative targets at least cost. Hypotheses: distribution data exist for the features, targets are set, and site costs are known. Complementarity means a site's value depends on the sites already chosen. - EV.O.A4.2.3 Eradication and suppression. Eradication is feasible only if every individual is at risk, removal exceeds replacement at all densities, and reinvasion is prevented. Suppression to a

threshold density is a different goal (uses EV.O.A1.4). - EV.O.A4.2.4 Translocation and viability analysis. A translocation succeeds when a self-sustaining population results after a stated period. Population viability analysis estimates extinction risk from demographic rates. Hypotheses: rates are estimated without large error, and stochasticity and catastrophes are modelled. Its absolute probabilities are CONTESTED; rankings of options are more robust (uses BI.O.A5.1). - EV.O.A4.3 Regulation and instruments — the policy is PO, the price instrument EC, the duty LA. **EV owns the measured environmental effect.** - EV.O.A4.3.1 Compliance and outcome. A

rule's compliance rate is not an environmental outcome. The claim must show a change in a pressure or a state attributable to the rule. That needs a counterfactual (W5). - EV.O.A4.3.2 Caps and leakage. A cap is judged by emissions under it against a counterfactual path. Leakage is displacement of emissions to uncovered places or periods. Market design is EC (uses EC.O.A5.3). The political cause is PO.O.A4.4. - EV.O.A4.3.3 Impact assessment as procedure. Environmental impact assessment predicts the effects of a proposal and its alternatives. Hypotheses: the proposal and alternatives

are defined, and baseline conditions are surveyed. A prediction audit compares each predicted effect with later monitoring. The legal requirement is LA.O.A1.1. - EV.O.A4.3.4 Treaties and controlled substances. The effect of a treaty is the change in a pressure it controls. The Montreal Protocol's control of ozone-depleting substances is a cited case, and its production record needs a source (UNVERIFIED). Recovery of the ozone state is a separate, later claim. Legal force is LA.O.A1.4; the institution is PO.O.A5.2. - EV.O.A4.7 Environmental engineering — technical work that changes a pressure or

a state. **An engineering response is a designed works or process, judged by measured performance against a specification.** Measurement, monitoring, and assessment are methods (EV.M.1 and EV.M.2), not a response cell. - EV.O.A4.7.1 Treatment performance. A treatment works is judged by removal efficiency, (inflow − outflow) / inflow, over a stated period. Efficiency varies with load and temperature. The reaction kinetics are CH.O.A4.1; the unit operation is EN. - EV.O.A4.7.2 Comparing options by life cycle. Life cycle assessment totals burdens from raw material to disposal (ISO 14040). Hypotheses: a functional

unit is defined, the boundary is stated, and inventory data represent the processes. Burden shifting between impact categories is its main defeater (EV.M.5). - EV.O.A4.7.3 Stormwater and flood works. A works is designed to a return period, which states its annual exceedance probability. It does not protect against larger events. The design event comes from EV.O.A2.6 and the hydraulics from EN.O.A2.3. - EV.O.A4.7.4 Waste flows. A waste system is described by a material flow analysis of tonnes in, recovered and disposed. A recycling rate must state whether it counts mass

collected or mass reprocessed. The waste hierarchy is a heuristic, not evidence of lower burden. - EV.O.A4.4 Kaitiakitanga in practice — guardianship as a response; its tradition-internal meaning is IK. No child cells are added here: IK content is not placed in this file pending Māori-led review (Standard v3). Named objects: restoration trajectory and reference state, bioremediation (degraders present, electron acceptor available, contaminant bioavailable), protected area effect (matched comparison), systematic conservation planning (distribution data, set targets, known costs), eradication criteria, population viability analysis (rates well estimated, stochasticity and catastrophes modelled;

CONTESTED for absolute risk), environmental impact assessment (defined proposal and alternatives, surveyed baseline), leakage, removal efficiency, life cycle assessment (functional unit, stated boundary, representative inventory), design return period, adaptive management (outcomes monitored, managers able to change course, competing hypotheses stated). ### EV.O.A5 Limits **SCQA.** Situation. Some values of a state or a pressure are treated as limits, set by a system property, by agreement or by law. Complication. A limit is partly a threshold in a system and partly a chosen value, and the two are often reported as one

number. Question. Where are the limits, and what kind of claim sets each? Answer. A limit claim states what fixes the value. It is a property of the system (a threshold), a choice (a standard) or a synthesis (a capacity or boundary). It names the warrant for that kind. Key line (inductive; plural noun: limits; dimension: what fixes the value; order: structural, from system property to chosen value to composite). Members (3): Thresholds and tipping points · Standards and bottom lines · Carrying capacity and planetary boundaries. - EV.O.A5.1 Thresholds

and tipping points — a regime shift occurs past a critical value, assuming bistable dynamics (theory MA.O.A4). **A threshold claim says that a driver has a critical value past which the system moves to another regime, under stated dynamics.** - EV.O.A5.1.1 Alternative stable states. A regime shift needs two stable states over a range of the driver. Shallow lakes are a proposed case, clear or turbid. Demonstrations in field systems are few, and general bistability in ecosystems is CONTESTED (uses MA.O.A4). - EV.O.A5.1.2 Hysteresis. Under bistability the threshold for return

differs from the threshold for loss. Lowering a driver to its earlier value does not restore the earlier state. The test is to move the driver up and then down. - EV.O.A5.1.3 Early warning signals. Rising variance and autocorrelation precede a transition in models approaching a fold bifurcation. Whether such signals work in real systems is OPEN (uses MA.O.A4). - EV.O.A5.1.4 Climate tipping elements. Parts of the ice sheets and ocean circulation are proposed as tipping elements. Threshold values are model-dependent and OPEN (uses EA.O.A4.4, EA.O.A4.3). - EV.O.A5.2 Standards and

bottom lines — legal or agreed limits (W12; force LA). **A standard is a value fixed by agreement or law; its scientific basis and its legal force are separate claims.** - EV.O.A5.2.1 Health-based standards. A health guideline is derived from the exposure–response with uncertainty factors. A guideline is advisory; a standard is binding in a jurisdiction (force LA). Where no threshold has been identified, as for fine particles, the value is a chosen level, not a threshold. - EV.O.A5.2.2 Ecosystem-based standards. A protective concentration can be derived from a species

sensitivity distribution (EV.O.A3.1.1). The percentage of species to protect is a policy choice. The derivation holds only under that method's hypotheses. - EV.O.A5.2.3 Numeric bottom lines. A bottom line is an attribute value below which a water body is not to fall. It is set by a stated process and tested by monitoring. The NZ freshwater instrument that names national bottom lines is UNVERIFIED in detail. - EV.O.A5.2.4 Compliance statistics. A standard stated as a percentile or a mean needs a sampling frequency adequate to estimate it. A 95th-percentile standard

estimated from few samples has wide error. Sampling error can decide compliance (uses MA.O.A5). - EV.O.A5.3 Carrying capacity and planetary boundaries — the planetary boundaries framework (Rockström et al., 2009) is a proposed set, CONTESTED in its numbers. **A capacity or boundary claim aggregates thresholds and flows into one limit for a stated system and period.** - EV.O.A5.3.1 Carrying capacity. K in the logistic model is a fixed capacity under stated conditions (uses BI.O.A5.1). A human carrying capacity is not fixed, because technology, consumption and trade change it. Human capacity

figures are CONTESTED unless their assumptions are stated. - EV.O.A5.3.2 The nine boundary processes. The 2009 proposal has nine processes: climate change, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land-system change, biodiversity loss, aerosol loading and chemical pollution. Two of the nine lacked a quantified boundary in 2009 (UNVERIFIED which). Each has a control variable and a proposed value. - EV.O.A5.3.3 Boundary and uncertainty. A boundary is proposed on the safe side of the uncertainty around a threshold. It is a normative choice built on a scientific

estimate. Interaction between boundaries is OPEN. - EV.O.A5.3.4 Catchment and regional limits. A global boundary gives no catchment limit. A catchment load limit is the load at which a response variable meets its target, read from a load–response relationship. The target is a standard (EV.O.A5.2). Allocation among users is normative. Named objects: bistability and hysteresis (two stable states over a driver range), critical slowing down (approach to a fold bifurcation; OPEN in real systems), standard and guideline value, bottom line, percentile compliance, carrying capacity K (logistic growth, fixed resources), planetary
boundaries (Rockström et al., 2009; CONTESTED in numbers), safe operating space, load–response relationship.

## 2. Governing thought Information science is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five stages of a record's life: items, description, arrangement, retrieval, and preservation. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the stage in the life of a record.** Order: from creation to keeping. 1. Items 2. Description 3. Arrangement 4. Retrieval 5. Preservation ## 4. Face O — Objects ### IS.O.A1 Items **Situation.** Every claim about records presupposes a unit that can be named, counted and cited. Libraries, archives and

research data services each fix that unit in their own way. **Complication.** A book, a letter and a data set are not the same kind of unit. The cataloguing, archival and data communities use different models, and identifiers are issued for all three. **Question.** What counts as one record, and by what rule is it identified? **Answer.** IS owns the model of the unit and the rule of identity. The historian's criticism of a record's content is HI. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: units of record; dimension: the kind of

unit being identified; order: structure, from the abstract unit to the name that points to any unit). Members (4): Works and manifestations · Records as evidence · Data sets · Persistent identifiers. - **IS.O.A1.1 Works and manifestations.** **FRBR and its successor LRM distinguish four entities: work, expression, manifestation and item.** FRBR is the IFLA report of 1998 and LRM is the IFLA consolidation of 2017. Both are conceptual models, not data formats. - IS.O.A1.1.1 Work and expression. In FRBR a translation is a new expression of the same work, and

an adaptation into another medium is a new work. Cataloguers can disagree on borderline cases, so agreement can be measured. - IS.O.A1.1.2 Manifestation and item. Copies from one production share one manifestation description. Features of a single copy, such as annotation, binding or ownership history, belong to the item. - IS.O.A1.1.3 BIBFRAME entities. BIBFRAME is an RDF vocabulary with Work, Instance and Item and no separate expression entity. Whether this loses information that FRBR keeps is CONTESTED. A round-trip conversion test measures the loss. - **IS.O.A1.2 Records as evidence.** **An

archival record is evidence of an activity.** Its source criticism for history is HI. - IS.O.A1.2.1 Record characteristics. ISO 15489-1:2016 states that a record should be authentic, reliable, have integrity and be usable. A records system is tested against each term by audit (W12 with W4). - IS.O.A1.2.2 Life cycle and continuum. The life-cycle model places a record in successive phases from creation to disposal. Upward's records continuum treats creation, management and use as concurrent. CONTESTED: neither model has a decisive test, and they differ most for digital records. -

IS.O.A1.2.3 Diplomatics. Diplomatics analyses the form of a record to judge its authenticity. Mabillon's De re diplomatica (1681) founded it for medieval charters. Its use on current records is IS. CONTESTED: for historical documents the alternative home is HI.O.A1.4 (uses HI.O.A1.4). - IS.O.A1.2.4 Appraisal values. Schellenberg separated primary values to the creator from secondary values to others, the latter evidential and informational (Modern Archives, 1956). The retention decision is IS. A legal duty to retain is LA. - **IS.O.A1.3 Data sets.** **A research data set is an item with its

own identity, version and provenance.** - IS.O.A1.3.1 Versioned citation. A data set can change after deposit, so a citation must name a version or a retrieval date. The FORCE11 Joint Declaration of Data Citation Principles (2014) states eight principles, including persistence and specificity. - IS.O.A1.3.2 FAIR principles. FAIR (Wilkinson and others, 2016) asks that data be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. The principles are guidance and do not require data to be open. Compliance is assessed against a stated metric set. - IS.O.A1.3.3 Data set boundary. OPEN: no rule fixes

where one data set ends and the next begins, notably for continuously updated data. The depositor declares the boundary. A subset citation is tested by re-extracting the subset. - IS.O.A1.3.4 Provenance model. W3C PROV (2013) describes provenance as relations among entities, activities and agents. It assumes the activities were logged when they happened. A provenance record is a claim about the past, supported by logs (W7). - **IS.O.A1.4 Persistent identifiers.** **A persistent identifier is a string issued under a registry's rules, so its validity is a stipulation (W12).** Examples are

DOI, ORCID and ISBN. - IS.O.A1.4.1 Check digits. The last digit of an ISBN-13 makes a weighted sum, with weights 1 and 3 alternating, a multiple of 10. It detects every single-digit error and every adjacent transposition except where the two digits differ by 5. ISBN-10 uses modulus 11 and detects every adjacent transposition. The number theory is MA (uses MA.O.A2). - IS.O.A1.4.2 Persistence as service. A DOI persists only while its registrant keeps its metadata and target current. The DOI system is ISO 26324 and resolves through the Handle

System. The failure rate is measured by sampling resolution (W4). - IS.O.A1.4.3 Identifier scope. An identifier names one entity at a stated granularity. An ORCID identifier names one person's record, and duplicates can arise when one person registers twice. The duplicate rate is measurable by comparing records. Named objects: FRBR and LRM (conceptual models; they assume a catalogue's user tasks and the four entities as defined); BIBFRAME (RDF vocabulary; Work, Instance, Item); ISO 15489-1 record characteristics; records continuum; diplomatics; Schellenberg's values; FAIR principles (guidance, no formal hypotheses); PROV (activities were

logged at the time); ISBN check digits (fixed weights and modulus; random digit errors); DOI (registrant keeps the target current). ### IS.O.A2 Description **Situation.** A record is found through a description of it. Descriptions follow standards that fix the elements, the rules for filling them and the vocabulary of the values. **Complication.** Metadata schemes, cataloguing codes and subject vocabularies were built by different communities for different carriers. Mapping between them loses information. **Question.** What must a description state, by what rule, and in what form? **Answer.** IS owns the element

sets, the cataloguing rules, the subject vocabularies and their publication as linked data. The logic of the RDF layer is MA. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: description practices; dimension: the part of a description the claim concerns; order: structure, from the element set to its machine-readable form). Members (4): Metadata standards · Cataloguing rules · Subject indexing · Linked data. - **IS.O.A2.1 Metadata standards.** **A metadata standard stipulates which elements describe a resource and how they are encoded (W12).** Examples are Dublin Core and MARC. - IS.O.A2.1.1 Dublin Core elements.

The Dublin Core Metadata Element Set (ISO 15836) has fifteen elements. They are title, creator, subject, description, publisher, contributor, date, type, format, identifier, source, language, relation, coverage and rights. Each is optional and repeatable. - IS.O.A2.1.2 MARC 21 structure. A MARC record has a leader, a directory and variable fields. Data fields carry a three-digit tag, two indicator positions and coded subfields. ISO 2709 serialises the record. - IS.O.A2.1.3 Crosswalks. A crosswalk maps the elements of one scheme to another. It loses or merges information where element meanings differ. Loss

is measured by converting a record set and back, then comparing. - IS.O.A2.1.4 Application profiles. A profile selects and constrains elements from one or more schemes for one community. A record conforms when it meets the stated cardinalities and value rules, which a validator tests (W11). - **IS.O.A2.2 Cataloguing rules.** **Cataloguing rules prescribe how a resource is described and how its access points are chosen.** RDA is a current standard. - IS.O.A2.2.1 User tasks. FRBR names four user tasks for a catalogue: find, identify, select and obtain. LRM adds explore.

A rule is justified in so far as it supports a task, which is argued (W9). - IS.O.A2.2.2 Authority control. An authority record fixes one authorised form of a name and refers variants to it. The effect is tested by comparing name searches with and without authority records. The hypothesis is that the file is maintained. - IS.O.A2.2.3 Content, media and carrier types. RDA records content type, media type and carrier type. It replaces the optional general material designation of AACR2. The change separates what a resource says from the

physical form that carries it. - IS.O.A2.2.4 Cataloguer consistency. UNVERIFIED: agreement between cataloguers is higher for transcribed elements than for name and subject access points. Test by independent cataloguing of one sample. - **IS.O.A2.3 Subject indexing.** **Subject indexing assigns terms from a controlled vocabulary so that records on one subject meet under one term.** Examples are MeSH and LCSH. - IS.O.A2.3.1 Thesaurus relations. ISO 25964 defines three relations among terms: equivalence (USE and UF), hierarchical (BT and NT) and associative (RT). Hierarchical links are of three kinds: generic, partitive and

instance. Mixing kinds breaks the inference from a broad term to its narrower terms. - IS.O.A2.3.2 Pre- and post-coordination. A pre-coordinated heading, such as an LCSH heading with subdivisions, fixes a combination of concepts in advance. A post-coordinated system combines terms at search time and can match terms that belong to different parts of a record. - IS.O.A2.3.3 Exhaustivity and specificity. Exhaustivity is the number of subjects indexed per record. Specificity is how narrow the terms are. Higher exhaustivity tends to raise recall and lower precision. Higher specificity tends to

raise precision. These hold for a fixed vocabulary and searching practice. - IS.O.A2.3.4 Indexing consistency. Consistency is the share of terms that two indexers both assign to one record. Several formulas exist, so a report states which one it uses. Low consistency limits retrieval by controlled terms. - **IS.O.A2.4 Linked data.** **Linked data publishes descriptions as RDF statements about identified resources, and SKOS expresses vocabularies in that form.** The logic is MA.O.A1; the vocabulary is IS. - IS.O.A2.4.1 Four principles. Berners-Lee (2006) gave four rules. Name things with URIs. Use

HTTP URIs so that they can be looked up. Return useful information in standards such as RDF. Include links to other URIs. The rules are guidance (W12). - IS.O.A2.4.2 SKOS hierarchy. SKOS (W3C, 2009) represents concepts with preferred and alternative labels and broader, narrower and related links. The property skos:broader is not transitive by itself. The transitive closure is a separate property. - IS.O.A2.4.3 Open-world reading. RDF and OWL semantics treat a missing statement as unknown, not false. A closed-world check, such as a SHACL shapes test (W3C, 2017), finds

missing required data. The logic is MA (uses MA.O.A1). - IS.O.A2.4.4 Identity links. The property owl:sameAs states that two names denote one thing, so every property of one holds for the other. Using it for similar or related things licenses false inferences. A set of links is tested for inferences that contradict known facts. Named objects: Dublin Core (ISO 15836; elements are optional and repeatable); MARC 21 (ISO 2709 encoding); crosswalk (element meanings are comparable); application profile; RDA (user tasks as stated; applied by trained cataloguers); authority file (maintained); thesaurus

(ISO 25964; hierarchical links are of one kind); LCSH and MeSH; SKOS (concept schemes, not class axioms); RDF (open-world statements); SHACL (closed-world shapes); owl:sameAs (strict identity). ### IS.O.A3 Arrangement **Situation.** Descriptions must be organised so that related records are found together. A scheme fixes the groups, their order and the notation that marks them. **Complication.** A shelf has one order, but a work may concern several subjects. Schemes also grow by accretion, so classes overlap and residual classes appear. **Question.** By what principle does each arrangement place a record, and

does it place it once? **Answer.** IS owns schemes, facets, archival arrangement, ontologies and the application of a scheme to claims. Whether an ontology's commitments are true is PL. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: arrangement principles; dimension: what fixes an item's position; order: structure, from enumerated schedules, through combined facets and creator provenance, to axiomatised ontologies, then the application to claims). Members (5): Classification schemes · Faceted classification · Archival arrangement · Ontologies · This taxonomy. - **IS.O.A3.1 Classification schemes.** **A classification scheme assigns each item one class in a

stipulated hierarchy (W12).** Whether its classes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive is testable (W9 with W4). Examples are LCC, DDC, UDC and MSC. - IS.O.A3.1.1 Dewey Decimal. DDC (first published 1876) has ten main classes, each divided into ten divisions and each division into ten sections. Decimal notation limits each level to ten branches. Topics of unequal size can be forced into equal slots. - IS.O.A3.1.2 Library of Congress. LCC has 21 lettered main classes. Each class has its own schedule, maintained separately, so notation and depth differ between classes.

The scheme follows the Library's collection, which is literary warrant. - IS.O.A3.1.3 Exclusivity test. A scheme level is mutually exclusive if each item fits one class there. It is exhaustive if some class fits every item. The tests are the double-classing rate and the residual-class rate over a sample (W4). A residual class such as general records a failure of exhaustiveness. - IS.O.A3.1.4 Single location. A single-hierarchy scheme gives a work on two subjects one place. The second subject is reachable only through the catalogue. Browsing one class then finds

a subset of the relevant works. The share shelved elsewhere is measurable (W4). - **IS.O.A3.2 Faceted classification.** **A faceted scheme describes an item by independent facets combined at the time of classing.** Ranganathan's Colon Classification uses the PMEST facets. - IS.O.A3.2.1 PMEST. Colon Classification (1933) analyses a subject into Personality, Matter, Energy, Space and Time. CONTESTED: whether five categories suffice for all subjects. Other category lists have been proposed. - IS.O.A3.2.2 Facet independence. Facet analysis assumes that the facets of a domain are mutually exclusive and that the values within

each facet are too. It fails where one value is defined by another. Test by searching for items whose value in one facet depends on another. - IS.O.A3.2.3 Citation order. The order in which facets are combined fixes where an item files and what is collocated. Changing the order moves items. The order is a design decision (W12), not a fact about the subject. - IS.O.A3.2.4 Faceted search. A search interface offers facets as filters where records carry controlled values for each facet. A filter is only as complete as

the share of records with a value. Coverage is measurable (W4). - **IS.O.A3.3 Archival arrangement.** **Archival arrangement keeps records by their creator (respect des fonds) and in the order the creator gave them (original order).** - IS.O.A3.3.1 Provenance. Under respect des fonds, records of one creator are kept apart from those of other creators. A French instruction of 1841 (Natalis de Wailly) is the usual source. The test is whether each record can be assigned to one creating body. - IS.O.A3.3.2 Original order. Original order keeps records as the creator

arranged them, because that order is evidence of how the creator worked. Where no original order can be shown, the archivist imposes one and records that. The test is whether the order can be reconstructed from the creator's registers. - IS.O.A3.3.3 Multilevel description. ISAD(G) describes records in levels, such as fonds, series, file and item. Its four rules are description from the general to the particular, information relevant to the level, linking of descriptions, and non-repetition of information. Conformity is testable (W11). - IS.O.A3.3.4 Digital original order. OPEN: file names,

folders and dates in a digital collection may reflect software behaviour and not the creator's practice. Whether original order can be recovered from file-system metadata is tested case by case. - **IS.O.A3.4 Ontologies.** **An ontology is a formal specification of the classes and relations of a domain.** BFO and DOLCE are upper-level examples. Their philosophical commitments are PL. - IS.O.A3.4.1 Definition and test. Gruber (1993) defined an ontology as an explicit specification of a conceptualisation. An ontology is tested by the competency questions it must answer and by logical consistency.

A reasoner checks consistency (W11). The truth of its axioms about the domain is argued (W9). - IS.O.A3.4.2 OWL 2 DL. Reasoning in OWL 2 DL is decidable under restrictions on the use of complex roles. Reasoning in OWL 2 Full is not decidable. The proofs are MA (uses MA.O.A1). The cost class of reasoning is CS (uses CS.O.A2.3). - IS.O.A3.4.3 Upper-level ontologies. BFO divides entities into continuants and occurrents. DOLCE divides them into endurants and perdurants. CONTESTED: choosing between them is a philosophical commitment (uses PL.O.A1.1). Whether either improves

integration is tested by alignment studies. - IS.O.A3.4.4 Alignment. Ontology alignment is scored against reference alignments, as in the OAEI campaigns. The scores assume that the reference is correct and complete.
