A different reference gives different scores. - **IS.O.A3.5 This taxonomy.** **This taxonomy classifies claims, not documents, and each claim has one home.** Its reliability is tested by the placement protocol. - IS.O.A3.5.1 Unit of claim. The unit classified is a sentence-level claim, not a document or a topic. A compound sentence is split into atomic claims before placement (Standard

v3, section 4a). Test: two placers split one text and compare the claims. - IS.O.A3.5.2 One home. Each claim has one owning pyramid, face and cell, and other pyramids cite it. Independent placers can test the rule. OPEN: no agreement figure is held in this file. - IS.O.A3.5.3 Key-line discipline. Each level has two to five members, one named dimension, one order and no residual member. A script checks counts and repeated members (R2, R7). Whether the dimension chosen is the best one is argued (W9). - IS.O.A3.5.4 Protocol reliability.

The placement protocol is a classification procedure. Its reliability is the share of test claims placed in the cell a specialist would choose. OPEN: no such test is recorded here. Named objects: Dewey Decimal Classification (ten classes; decimal notation); Library of Congress Classification (21 classes; literary warrant); Universal Decimal Classification (synthesis by auxiliary signs); MSC; Colon Classification and PMEST (facets are independent); citation order; respect des fonds (a creator can be identified); original order (the order is evidence); ISAD(G) (levels are nested); OWL 2 DL (decidable under stated restrictions); BFO

and DOLCE (distinct upper-level commitments); OAEI alignment scores (reference is correct); this taxonomy's one-home rule. ### IS.O.A4 Retrieval **Situation.** Arranged records are useful only if the right ones can be found. Retrieval is tested by comparing what a system returns with what a judge calls relevant. **Complication.** Relevance depends on the person and the moment. Ranking algorithms are CS and the mind of the searcher is MS, so the claim about finding itself had no home. **Question.** How well are records found, by whom, and how is that measured? **Answer.**

IS owns the effectiveness measures, the concept of relevance, the quantitative laws of literatures and the models of seeking. The algorithm's cost is CS and the cognitive mechanism is MS. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: findability claims; dimension: what is measured about finding; order: structure, from the system's output to the judge, the literature and the seeker). Members (4): Retrieval effectiveness · Relevance · Bibliometrics · Information behaviour. - **IS.O.A4.1 Retrieval effectiveness.** **Retrieval effectiveness is measured by precision and recall against relevance judgements.** The algorithm's cost is CS. - IS.O.A4.1.1

Precision and recall. Precision is the share of retrieved items that are relevant. Recall is the share of relevant items that are retrieved. Recall needs the number of relevant items in the collection, which is unknown for large collections and is estimated. - IS.O.A4.1.2 Cranfield design. Cleverdon's Cranfield tests fixed a document collection, a set of topics and relevance judgements. The design assumes one judgement per document and topic holds across users. Transfer to real users is tested separately (W4). - IS.O.A4.1.3 Pooling. TREC (from 1992) judges the union of

the top results of the participating systems. It assumes that unjudged documents are not relevant. A system outside the pool can be underscored. Test by removing one participant's contribution and rescoring. - IS.O.A4.1.4 Rank-based measures. Average precision and nDCG score a ranked list. The nDCG measure (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002) uses graded relevance and a logarithmic discount by rank. The discount assumes a model of user attention, so the measure is valid for that model only. - **IS.O.A4.2 Relevance.** **Relevance is a judgement of a document against a need, as

topical relevance or user relevance.** Assessors make the judgement, so it is measured (W4). - IS.O.A4.2.1 Topical and user relevance. Topical relevance is whether a document is about the topic. User relevance is whether it is useful to this person in this situation. A test collection measures the first. - IS.O.A4.2.2 Assessor disagreement. Different assessors judge the same documents differently. Voorhees (2000) reported that system rankings stayed largely stable under such variation, although absolute scores changed. UNVERIFIED: the extent of the stability. Test by swapping assessor sets. - IS.O.A4.2.3 Graded

relevance. Judgements on a scale, such as not, partly and highly relevant, are ordinal. Averaging grades treats them as interval. The gain values assigned to grades are stipulations (W12) and change the value of a measure. - IS.O.A4.2.4 Relevance feedback. Rocchio (1971) moves a query towards documents judged relevant and away from those judged not relevant, in a vector space. It assumes relevant documents resemble each other in term space. The gain is IS; the algorithm's cost is CS. - **IS.O.A4.3 Bibliometrics.** **Lotka's law (author productivity) and Bradford's law (scattering)

are empirical regularities within stated literatures.** - IS.O.A4.3.1 Lotka's law. Lotka (1926) found that the number of authors with n publications falls roughly as 1/n² in the literatures he studied. The exponent varies between literatures. The fit is tested in each literature (W4). - IS.O.A4.3.2 Bradford's law. Bradford (1934) ranked journals by yield on one subject. He found zones that each gave the same number of articles. The journal counts in the zones stand in the ratio 1 : n : n². The law is stated for a single subject

bibliography. It is a regularity, not a derivation. - IS.O.A4.3.3 Citation analysis. Citation counts indicate use by authors, not quality. Citing practice differs by field and year, so counts are normalised. Counts compare only works of comparable field and age. - IS.O.A4.3.4 Indicators. The h-index (Hirsch, 2005) is the largest h such that h of an author's papers have at least h citations each. It ignores field and career length. Citation distributions are skewed, so a journal's mean citation rate can differ from a typical article's. - **IS.O.A4.4 Information behaviour.**

**Information behaviour is how people identify a need, seek information and use it.** The cognitive mechanism is MS. - IS.O.A4.4.1 Information search process. Kuhlthau's model has six stages: initiation, selection, exploration, formulation, collection and presentation. It holds that uncertainty is high early and falls after formulation. UNVERIFIED: the evidence base is mainly students in library tasks. CONTESTED: its generality. - IS.O.A4.4.2 Berrypicking. Bates (1989) argued that a query evolves as the searcher reads and that information is gathered in pieces from varied sources. This conflicts with the fixed query in

the Cranfield design. Log studies of query reformulation test it (W4). - IS.O.A4.4.3 Information foraging. Pirolli and Card (1999) model searchers as maximising information gained per unit cost, guided by cues called information scent. The model assumes the searcher can estimate cost and gain. It is tested by comparing predicted and observed paths. - IS.O.A4.4.4 Information need. Taylor described four levels of need, from the unexpressed to the formal question. Belkin's anomalous state of knowledge holds that a searcher cannot fully specify what is missing. Both imply that a query

is an imperfect expression of need. Named objects: precision and recall (relevance judgements exist for a test collection); Cranfield design (judgements transfer across users); pooling (unjudged documents are not relevant); average precision and nDCG (a user model of attention); BM25 (terms are independent; parameters are tuned to the collection); inverse document frequency (Spärck Jones 1972; rare terms discriminate); Rocchio feedback (relevant documents are similar); Lotka's law; Bradford's law; h-index; Information Search Process; berrypicking; information foraging (searcher maximises gain per cost); anomalous state of knowledge. ### IS.O.A5 Preservation **Situation.** Records outlast

their creators only if their carriers, formats and rights are managed. Keeping a record usable is a continuing activity, not a state. **Complication.** Paper decays chemically, digital files depend on software, and access is limited by law and consent. The claims were spread across chemistry, computer science and law. **Question.** What must be kept for a record to stay usable, and who may use it? **Answer.** IS owns the rules for keeping the carrier and the content, and for stating access. The chemistry is CH, the licence law is LA,

and tradition-internal authority over Indigenous data is IK. **Key line** (inductive; plural noun: preservation claims; dimension: the threat or limit to continued use; order: structure, from the physical carrier to the digital object, then rights, then governance). Members (4): Physical conservation · Digital preservation · Access and rights · Indigenous data governance. - **IS.O.A5.1 Physical conservation.** **Physical conservation slows the decay of the material carrier.** The chemistry of paper and media is CH. - IS.O.A5.1.1 Agents of deterioration. The Canadian Conservation Institute lists ten agents. They are physical forces; thieves,

vandals and displacers; fire; water; pests; contaminants; light, ultraviolet and infrared radiation; incorrect temperature; incorrect relative humidity; and dissociation. Preventive conservation controls them, and each can be audited. - IS.O.A5.1.2 Storage conditions. The decay of paper and film slows at lower temperature and lower relative humidity. Over a narrow range the rate follows the Arrhenius form (uses CH.O.A4.2). A storage specification states set points with tolerances (W12). - IS.O.A5.1.3 Intervention. Conservation codes ask for documented treatment and minimal intervention. Reversibility is often stated as a goal. CONTESTED: some treatments cannot

be reversed, and retreatability is proposed in its place. - IS.O.A5.1.4 Media decay. Cellulose acetate film decays by hydrolysis that releases acetic acid and speeds further decay, called vinegar syndrome. The binder of magnetic tape can hydrolyse and shed or stick. Each medium has a dominant mechanism, so a storage rule names the medium (uses CH.O.A4). - **IS.O.A5.2 Digital preservation.** **Digital preservation keeps digital objects usable over time, and the OAIS reference model (ISO 14721) stipulates its functions (W12).** - IS.O.A5.2.1 OAIS entities. OAIS has six functional entities: ingest, archival

storage, data management, administration, preservation planning and access. Content moves as submission, archival and dissemination information packages. An archive claims conformance by mapping its functions to these (W11). - IS.O.A5.2.2 Designated community. OAIS defines success relative to a designated community whose knowledge base is stated. When that knowledge changes, more representation information is needed. The claim assumes the community can be identified. - IS.O.A5.2.3 Migration and emulation. Migration converts the bitstream to a current format. Emulation keeps the bitstream and reproduces the software environment. Each can lose properties that matter.

CONTESTED: which properties are significant, since that depends on the user. Compare rendered output before and after (W4). - IS.O.A5.2.4 Fixity and copies. A stored checksum detects change in a copy. With several independent copies, a corrupted copy can be found and replaced from an intact one. This assumes a collision-resistant hash and independent failures (uses CS.O.A5.1). - **IS.O.A5.3 Access and rights.** **Access and rights state who may read and reuse a record, including through open access.** Copyright is LA. - IS.O.A5.3.1 Gold and green. Gold open access publishes the

work openly at the publisher. Green open access deposits a version in a repository. The share of each varies by field and year, so any share needs a stated sample (W4). - IS.O.A5.3.2 Licence statements. A licence such as Creative Commons Attribution states permitted reuse. Whether the licence is valid in law is LA. Whether a record carries a clear, machine-readable licence statement is IS, and an audit tests it. - IS.O.A5.3.3 Conditions of access. ISAD(G) has a description element for conditions governing access. A closure period or restriction on

a record is recorded there, and its legal basis is LA. Test by sampling closed records for a stated condition. - IS.O.A5.4 Indigenous data governance — the CARE principles; Māori data sovereignty (Te Mana Raraunga). Tradition-internal authority over the data is IK. Held as first written; no content is added here, and the Māori-led review gate in Standard v3 applies. Named objects: Canadian Conservation Institute agents of deterioration (a stated list); Arrhenius rate dependence (a narrow temperature range; one dominant reaction); vinegar syndrome (acetate base); OAIS (a designated community is

identified); submission, archival and dissemination packages; ISO 16363 (audit of trustworthy digital repositories); fixity checksum (stored apart from the file; recomputed on a schedule); migration; emulation; gold and green open access; Creative Commons licences; ISAD(G) access element.

## 2. Governing thought Indigenous knowledge is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five aspects of a knowledge system: ordering principles, relations to land and waters, governance and custom, transmission, and research and data. ## 3. Key line Dimension: **the aspect of a knowledge system the claim is about.** Order: from the system's principles to its relation with outside research. 1. Ordering principles 2. Relations to land and waters 3. Governance and custom 4. Transmission 5. Research and data A

people (iwi, hapū, nation) is a substrate, not a cell. A ·M sentence names its iwi or hapū, because authority is local. ## 4. Face O — Objects ### IK.O.A1 Ordering principles **SCQA.** A knowledge system orders the world by its own principles. What are they, as held? Key line: whakapapa as an ordering principle, categories of status, cyclical time. - IK.O.A1.1 Whakapapa as ordering — genealogy as the principle that relates people, atua and the natural world. Whakapapa as human descent is HI; whakapapa of atua is RE. -

IK.O.A1.2 Categories of status — tapu and noa as ordering categories outside rite (in rite, RE.O.A1.2). - IK.O.A1.3 Cyclical and ancestral time — "ka mua, ka muri" (walking backwards into the future) as a stated orientation (·S W8; ·M W13). ### IK.O.A2 Relations to land and waters **SCQA.** Knowledge systems hold relations to particular places. What is claimed about that relation? Key line: kaitiakitanga, maramataka, place knowledge. - IK.O.A2.1 Kaitiakitanga — guardianship as obligation. Its measured environmental effect is EV.O.A4.4. - IK.O.A2.2 Maramataka — the lunar calendar as a system

for timing activity. An ecological observation it records (a fish run) is BI or EA under W4; the system itself is IK. - IK.O.A2.3 Place knowledge — names, boundaries and histories of places, held by mana whenua. The landform is EA; the dated event is HI. ### IK.O.A3 Governance and custom **SCQA.** Communities govern themselves by custom and authority. Key line: tikanga as custom, rangatiratanga, marae kawa, customary institutions. - IK.O.A3.1 Tikanga as custom — correct practice in social life. In rite before atua it is RE.O.A3.1. As recognised by

a state court it is LA.O.A1.3. - IK.O.A3.2 Rangatiratanga — authority and self-determination as held. Its Treaty and legal dimension is LA.O.A4.4; its political dimension is PO. - IK.O.A3.3 Marae kawa — the protocols of a particular marae (local, ·M). - IK.O.A3.4 Customary institutions — rūnanga, hui as decision forums. ### IK.O.A4 Transmission **SCQA.** Knowledge lives only if transmitted. How is it passed on, and who may hold it? Key line: institutions of learning, oral and performed transmission, restricted knowledge. - IK.O.A4.1 Institutions of learning — whare wānanga, past and

present. Modern wānanga as tertiary institutions are ED. - IK.O.A4.2 Oral and performed transmission — kōrero tuku iho, mōteatea, haka. Their poetics are AR; their language is LN. - IK.O.A4.3 Restricted knowledge — knowledge held by designated people and not for open classification. The pyramid records that restriction exists, never the content. ### IK.O.A5 Research and data **SCQA.** Outside research has often taken Indigenous knowledge without consent. What rules govern research and data? Key line: Kaupapa Māori research, data sovereignty, consent and benefit. - IK.O.A5.1 Kaupapa Māori research — research

by, with and for Māori, under Māori control (Smith, *Decolonizing Methodologies*, 1999). - IK.O.A5.2 Data sovereignty — Te Mana Raraunga principles; the CARE principles. The records framework is IS.O.A5.4. - IK.O.A5.3 Consent and benefit — Wai 262 (*Ko Aotearoa Tēnei*, 2011) on flora, fauna and mātauranga (UNVERIFIED date). Legal effect is LA.
